429: The Google Ads API is a programmatic interface for managing Google Ads accounts and campaigns, suitable for large or complex setups.
430: Typical uses of the Google Ads API include automated account management, custom reporting, ad management based on inventory, and Smart Bidding strategy management.
431: The Google Ads API is recommended for developers comfortable with writing code and managing their own software infrastructure.
432: Google Ads scripts, BigQuery Data Transfer service, automated rules, bulk uploads, and Google Ads Editor are alternative tools for automating Google Ads for different needs and technical skill levels.
433: The Google Ads API is the programmatic interface to Google Ads, used for managing large or
434: complex Google Ads accounts and campaigns. You can build software that manages
435: accounts from the customer level down to the keyword level. Typical use cases
436: include:
437: Automated account management:
438: Create and link accounts, manage account hierarchies, and automate user
439: access.
440: Custom reporting: Query performance metrics,
441: segments, and resource attributes using the
442: Google Ads Query Language (GAQL).
443: Campaign and inventory-based ad management:
444: Create and update Performance Max,
445: Search,
446: Demand Gen,
447: Shopping,
448: Video, and
449: App campaigns,
450: budgets, and
451: assets.
452: Conversion measurement and
453: Smart Bidding strategy management:
454: Upload click, call, and enhanced conversions and configure automated bidding
455: strategies.

429: Google Ads API utilizes the OAuth 2.0 protocol for authentication and authorization, allowing your app to access user accounts without handling login information.
430: In addition to OAuth 2.0 credentials, a developer token is also required to make Google Ads API calls.
431: While all Google-supported OAuth 2.0 scenarios work, this guide focuses on the most common ones for Google Ads API developers.
432: The recommended OAuth 2.0 approach depends on your specific application scenario, such as integrating with existing Google APIs, managing your own accounts, or managing accounts on behalf of other users.
433: Note: You should configure your OAuth credentials using the same Google Cloud
434: project where you have enabled the
435: Google Ads API and requested an appropriate
436: API access level for the Google Ads API to work
437: correctly.
438: Just like other Google APIs, Google Ads API uses the OAuth 2.0 protocol
439: for authentication and authorization. OAuth 2.0 enables your Google Ads API client app
440: to access a user's Google Ads account without having to handle or store the user's
441: login info.
442: Broadly speaking, all the OAuth 2.0 authorization scenarios
443: that Google supports also work with Google Ads API. However, this guide focuses on the
444: scenarios that are most common for Google Ads API developers.

58: outlined_flag
59: Google Ads API developer tokens have an access level determining production account access and operation limits, and "permissible use" defining allowed API features.
60: There are three access levels: Test Account Access for test accounts with a 15,000 operation limit, Basic Access for test and production accounts with a 15,000 operation limit, and Standard Access for test and production accounts with an unlimited operation limit.
61: You start with Test Account Access and can apply to increase your access level through additional steps.
62: Permissible use, applicable to Basic and Standard Access, is based on intended API use and determines specific feature access like ad creation/management, reporting, or keyword research.
63: Your Google Cloud project is assigned an access level and "permissible use." The
64: access level determines whether you can affect production accounts and the
65: number of operations and requests that you can execute daily. Permissible
66: use determines the specific Google Ads API features that the project is allowed to
67: use.
68: Key Point: Getting started with the Google Ads API? Developer tokens were
69: sunset on September 9, 2026, and API access levels are now managed
70: per Google Cloud project. After you enable the Google Ads API
71: (which grants Test access), you can immediately apply on
72: the Google Ads API Overview page in the Google Cloud Console for
73: Explorer access (automated review and approval in
74: most cases, for up to 2,880 operations per day against production accounts). For
75: end-to-end setup, see the Make your first call quickstart or
76: the Google Ads MCP server guide.
77: Go to Google Ads API Overview in
78: Cloud Console
79: Access levels
80: There are four different API access levels listed in order in the
81: table. If you don't already have Google Ads API access, you can start by
82: enabling the API to obtain Test access
83: level for your Google Cloud project, and then apply for Explorer
84: access on the Google Ads API Overview page to access
85: production accounts.

113: Test access
114: After you've enabled Google Ads API, your Google Cloud project is granted Test access.
115: This means that the project can only make Google Ads API requests against test
116: accounts.
117: Important: Refer to the test account guide to learn more about
118: how to create a test account.
119: Apply for Test access

121: in your Google Cloud project to automatically be granted Test access for your
122: project.
123: Explorer access level
124: After you've completed the initial sign-up for the Google Ads API, Google may let you
125: apply for Explorer access level.
126: The Explorer access level allows your Google Cloud project to make Google Ads API
127: requests against both test accounts and production accounts. Production
128: accounts are any accounts that serve real, live Google ads—test accounts
129: don't serve ads.
130: The Explorer access level allows your Google Cloud project to execute up to
131: 2,880 operations per day against production accounts. This is sufficient for
132: most developers to get started with the API and build basic automation.
133: The Explorer access level restricts access to the following features. If you
134: need to use these features, you need to apply for
135: Basic access level or Standard access level.

169: after you submit your application.
170: Basic access level
171: The Basic access level allows your Google Cloud project to make Google Ads API requests
172: against both test accounts and production accounts. Production accounts are
173: any accounts that serve real, live Google ads—test accounts don't serve
174: ads.
175: The Basic access level allows your Google Cloud project to execute up to 15,000
176: operations per day. This is sufficient for most developers.
177: Apply for Basic access level
178: Note: Completing brand verification for your Google Cloud project is a
179: prerequisite to apply for Basic access level. Refer to the brand verification
180: guide to learn more.
181: Navigate to the Google Ads API Overview page in your Google Cloud
182: project.
183: Verify that the page displays your current access level as Explorer.
184: Click to expand the Upgrade access level section.
185: Confirm that the Next access level is displayed as Basic.
186: Confirm that there are no warnings indicating that you haven't completed
187: brand verification for your project. If there are,
188: follow the instructions to complete brand verification
189: before continuing.
190: Click the Apply for access button to apply for Basic access level.
191: Google may automatically upgrade your project's API access level to Basic
192: once you submit your application.
193: Standard access level
194: Standard access level allows your Google Cloud project to execute an unlimited
195: number of operations per day for all services. Individual services and features
196: may still have rate limits and restrictions that are specific to
197: those features, which will continue to apply even if your project has Standard
198: access level.
199: The Standard access level is only granted to developers who require unlimited
200: Google Ads API operations, such as large companies or tools that serve many users.
201: Apply for Standard access level
202: Navigate to the Google Ads API Overview page in your Google Cloud
203: project.
204: Verify that the page displays your current access level as Basic.
205: Click to expand the Upgrade access level section.
206: Confirm that the Next access level is displayed as Standard.
207: Click the Start application button to start the Standard access level
208: application.
209: The Standard access application involves a detailed manual audit of your
210: application. Be prepared to answer questions about your tool's functionality and
211: its target audience. If your tool is used by external users, be prepared to
212: provide demo sign-in access to your tool. Note that your tool must comply with
213: the Required Minimum Functionality.
214: Throughout the review process, the Google Compliance team will communicate with
215: you using your email address. Make sure you respond promptly to the queries from
216: the Compliance team to make progress with your Standard access application. When
217: the review is complete, Google will email you with the final outcome of the
218: review process.
219: API quotas and system rate limits
220: Regardless of the access level, all API operations are subject to system rate
221: limits, which restricts how many operations you may perform in a period of time,
222: that is the number of operations per hour. To learn more about how to handle
223: rate limit errors, see error types.
224: Individual services may enforce additional limits and quota restrictions due to
225: reasons such as product design limitations, product policy restrictions, API
226: performance and latency considerations. See the documentation about API
227: quotas to learn more about these restrictions.
228: Permissible use
229: Permissible use only applies to Google Cloud projects with Standard access
230: level. Permissible use is allocated based on intended use of the Google Ads API. These
231: permissions determine which features of the API your tool can use, as
232: elaborated in the following table:
233: Permissible Use
234: Description
235: Ad creation / management
236: Provide access to all services of the API for creating and managing Google Ads campaigns, ad groups, ads, and keywords.
237: Reporting
238: Only make GoogleAdsService.Search or GoogleAdsService.SearchStream requests, or read-only calls. This is for developers who only use the API to request stats.
239: Researching keywords and recommendations
240: Allow the Google Cloud project to access RecommendationService, KeywordPlanIdeaService, and KeywordPlanService. This is only used by tools requiring suggestions to help facilitate the creation and management of Google Ads campaigns.
241: Change permissible use
242: If your Google Cloud project has been approved for Standard access level, you
243: can fill out the application to update permissible use. Fill out
244: the application if you would like to update your permissible use or grant your
245: clients access to your tool.

429: Testing is crucial for a successful Google Ads API integration, covering development, maintenance, and new features.
430: You can use test accounts for most development purposes, but production accounts are needed to test features like performance reports due to test account limitations.
431: It is recommended to maintain separate test credentials from production credentials to minimize the risk of accidental modifications to production accounts during testing.
432: The validate_only field can be used to check if a request is valid without executing it.
433: The REST API, including curl and the REST explorer, is useful for ad hoc testing to validate expected output.
434: Testing is an important step in building a successful Google Ads API integration,
435: whether you're just getting started, maintaining an app, or adding new features
436: to an existing integration. This guide presents some best practices for testing
437: your Google Ads API integration.
438: Test accounts and production accounts
439: Note on Test Account Retention:
440: Google Ads API test accounts and their associated data are subject to automatic deletion. Any test account that remains inactive (has no API activity or logins) for a continuous period of one year will be permanently removed.
441: To prevent unintended deletion, ensure you interact with your test accounts periodically if you want to retain them.
442: Test accounts are available for development purposes. With test
443: accounts, you can validate that your application code and configuration are
444: working as intended.
445: However, not all features can be tested in a test
446: account.
447: When test account limitations prevent you from testing some features in your
448: integration, you can instead use a production account for development. Your
449: Google Cloud project must have at least the
450: Explorer access level (Explorer, Basic, or Standard) to
451: call a production account. Note that Explorer access still restricts certain
452: services—including billing (BillingSetupService
453: and AccountBudgetProposalService),
454: planning, account creation, and user invitations (see Explorer feature
455: restrictions)—which require Basic or Standard
456: access. Attempting to call a production account from a
457: project with the Test access level returns
458: AuthorizationError.CLOUD_PROJECT_NOT_APPROVED_FOR_PRODUCTION
459: starting in v25, or
460: AuthorizationError.ACTION_NOT_PERMITTED in v24 and
461: earlier.
462: Production accounts for development differ from test accounts in the following
463: ways:
464: Serve ads that can be seen by users
465: Require valid URLs
466: Must comply with advertising policies
467: Because production accounts serve ads, they generate metrics letting you test
468: performance reports, as well as unlocking all the other features of the Google Ads API.
469: However, using them for development requires extra caution. We recommend taking
470: the following measures:
471: Only grant access to users that need it for development purposes.
472: Set a fixed, low daily account budget.
473: Use production accounts for development only when test accounts can't be
474: used.
475: Thus, to do full testing of your integration, you will likely need both test
476: credentials and production credentials.
477: Test credentials
478: To minimize the risk of accidentally modifying production accounts when trying
479: to modify development accounts, we recommend maintaining a set of test
480: credentials that are separate from your production application credentials.
481: To create a set of test credentials, follow these steps:
482: Create an email account (for example, api.test@example.com) or a service
483: account that will be used only for testing purposes.
484: Add this user or service account as a valid user in the Google Ads accounts you
485: are running your tests against. Make sure you give appropriate access
486: levels to this user or service account. Don't give this
487: user or service account access to any production accounts.
488: If you are using the OAuth 2.0 user authentication flow, rather than the
489: service account flow, then generate a refresh token for
490: your test user account.
491: Use these new credentials when testing your application. The client ID and
492: client secret can be reused for testing purposes, since they have no effect
493: in determining which Google Ads accounts can be accessed. Store all credentials
494: and refresh tokens securely, and never commit them to source control.
495: Request validation
496: If you just need to test whether a request is valid—for example, to verify
497: that the request is structured correctly and does not violate policies—you
498: can use the validate_only field, which is available for
499: GoogleAdsService.Search requests (note that
500: GoogleAdsService.SearchStream does not support
501: validate_only) and most mutate requests. Consult the
502: reference documentation to verify whether this field is
503: available for a given method.
504: Note: Starting in v25, Performance Max campaign generation for Smart
505: campaigns does not support validate_only mode and returns
506: SmartCampaignError.VALIDATE_ONLY_GENERATE_PMAX_NOT_SUPPORTED
507: if validate_only is set to true.
508: REST API
509: For ad hoc testing, for example to validate that a request yields the expected
510: output, using the REST API is often the easiest option. Consult the REST
511: examples to learn how to use curl in making requests to the REST
512: API. Also, try testing in the REST explorer.

428: outlined_flag
429: The Google Ads API consists of resources, which represent entities, and services, which retrieve and manipulate them.
430: A Google Ads account is organized hierarchically, starting with the customer at the top level, followed by campaigns, ad groups, and ad group ads.
431: Every object in Google Ads is identified by an ID, and resources also have a unique resource_name string.
432: Services allow you to modify objects using mutate requests, retrieve objects and performance statistics with GoogleAdsService, and retrieve metadata with GoogleAdsFieldService.
433: This guide introduces the primary components that make up the Google Ads API. The
434: Google Ads API consists of resources and services. A resource represents a Google Ads
435: entity, while services retrieve and manipulate Google Ads entities.
436: Object hierarchy
437: A Google Ads account can be viewed as a hierarchy of objects.
438: The top-level resource of an account is the
439: customer.
440: Each customer contains one or more active
441: campaigns.
442: Each campaign contains one or more ad groups, used
443: to group your ads into logical collections.
444: An ad group ad represents an ad that you're
445: running in an ad group. Except for App campaigns, which can have only one ad
446: group ad per ad group, each ad group contains one or more ad group ads.
447: Performance Max campaigns use a different
448: structure from other campaign types: instead of ad groups and ad group ads, a
449: Performance Max campaign contains asset groups. You
450: link creative assets to an asset group using
451: AssetGroupAsset and attach audience or search
452: theme signals using AssetGroupSignal.
453: You can attach one or more AdGroupCriterion
454: or CampaignCriterion resources to an ad
455: group or campaign. These represent criteria that define how ads get triggered.
456: There are many criterion types,
457: such as keywords, age ranges, and locations. Criteria defined at the campaign
458: level affect all other resources within the campaign. You can also specify
459: budgets as well as start and end dates and times for campaigns, or for
460: individual ads using AdGroupAd.start_date_time and AdGroupAd.end_date_time.
461: Finally, you can attach assets at the account, campaign, ad group, or asset
462: group level. Assets let you provide extra information to your ads, like phone
463: numbers, street addresses, or promotions. See Assets
464: overview.
465: Resources
466: Resources represent the entities within your Google Ads account.
467: Campaign and AdGroup are
468: two examples of resources.
469: Object IDs
470: Every object in Google Ads is identified by its own ID. Some of these IDs are
471: globally unique across all Google Ads accounts, while others are unique only within
472: a confined scope.
473: Object ID
474: Scope of uniqueness
475: Globally unique?
476: Budget ID
477: Global
478: Yes
479: Campaign ID
480: Global
481: Yes
482: AdGroup ID
483: Global
484: Yes
485: Ad ID
486: Ad group
487: No, but (AdGroupId, AdId) pair is globally unique. Sharing an AdId across multiple ad groups is prohibited.
488: AdGroupCriterion ID
489: Ad group
490: No, but (AdGroupId, CriterionId) pair is globally unique
491: CampaignCriterion ID
492: Campaign
493: No, but (CampaignId, CriterionId) pair is globally unique
494: Label ID
495: Customer
496: No, but (CustomerId, LabelId) pair is globally unique
497: UserList ID
498: Global
499: Yes
500: Asset ID
501: Global
502: Yes
503: These ID rules can be useful when designing local storage for your Google Ads
504: objects.
505: Some objects can be used for multiple entity types. In such cases, the object
506: contains a type field that describes its contents. For example,
507: AdGroupAd can refer to an object such as a
508: responsive search ad, hotel ad, or Demand Gen ad. This value can be accessed
509: through the AdGroupAd.ad.type field, and returns a
510: value in the AdType enum. Note that
511: mutability can vary by version (for example, VideoResponsiveAdInfo on Ad is
512: mutable in v24 and later).
513: Resource names
514: Each resource is uniquely identified by a resource_name string that
515: concatenates the resource and its parents into a path. For example, campaign
516: resource names have the form:
517: customers/customer_id/campaigns/campaign_id
518: So for a campaign with ID 987654 in the Google Ads account with customer ID
519: 1234567, the resource_name would be:
520: customers/1234567/campaigns/987654
521: Services
522: Services let you retrieve and modify your Google Ads entities. There are three types
523: of services: modification, object and stat retrieval, and metadata retrieval
524: services.
525: Modify (mutate) objects
526: Resource-specific services modify instances of an associated resource type using
527: a mutate request. You can also use
528: GoogleAdsService.Mutate to perform atomic
529: mutations across multiple resource types in a single request (such as creating a
530: campaign budget, campaign, and ad group together).
531: Key Point: Retrieve objects and performance data using
532: GoogleAdsService with a Google Ads Query Language query.
533: Examples of resource-specific services:
534: CustomerService for modifying
535: customers.
536: CampaignService for modifying
537: campaigns.
538: AdGroupService for modifying
539: ad groups.
540: Each mutate request must include corresponding operation objects. For
541: example, the CampaignService.MutateCampaigns method expects one or more
542: instances of CampaignOperation. See
543: Change objects for a detailed discussion of
544: operations.
545: Concurrent mutates
546: A Google Ads object cannot be modified concurrently by more than one source. This
547: could cause errors to arise if you have multiple users updating the same object
548: with your app, or if you're mutating Google Ads objects in parallel using multiple
549: threads. This includes updating the object from multiple threads in the same
550: application, or from different applications (for example, your app and a
551: simultaneous Google Ads UI session).
552: The API does not provide a way to lock an object before updating; if two sources
553: try to simultaneously mutate an object, the API raises a
554: DatabaseError.CONCURRENT_MODIFICATION error.
555: Asynchronous versus synchronous mutates
556: The Google Ads API mutate methods are synchronous. API calls return a response only
557: after the objects are mutated, requiring you to wait for a response to each
558: request. While this approach is relatively straightforward to code, it could
559: negatively impact load balancing and waste resources if processes are forced to
560: wait for calls to complete.
561: An alternate approach is to mutate objects asynchronously using
562: BatchJobService, which performs batches of
563: operations on multiple services without waiting for their completion. Once a
564: batch job is submitted, Google Ads API servers execute operations asynchronously,
565: freeing processes to perform other operations. You can periodically check the
566: job status for completion.
567: See the Batch processing guide for more on
568: asynchronous processing.
569: Mutate validation
570: Most mutate requests can be validated without actually executing the call
571: against real data. You can test the request for missing parameters and incorrect
572: field values without actually executing the operation.
573: To use this feature, set the request's optional validate_only boolean field to
574: true. The request is fully validated as if it were going to be executed, but
575: the final execution is skipped. If no errors are found, the response is returned
576: with no mutated results populated (results is empty). If validation fails, the
577: request fails with a GoogleAdsFailure RPC
578: error by default (partial_failure = false), or returns a normal response with
579: operation-specific errors in partial_failure_error when
580: partial_failure = true.
581: validate_only is particularly useful in testing ads for common policy
582: violations. Ads are automatically rejected if they violate policies such as
583: having specific words, punctuation, capitalization, or length. A single bad ad
584: could cause an entire batch to fail. Testing a new ad within a validate_only
585: request can reveal any such violations. Refer to the code example for handling
586: policy violation errors to see
587: this in action.
588: Get objects and performance stats
589: GoogleAdsService is the single, unified
590: service for retrieving objects and performance statistics.
591: All Search and
592: SearchStream requests for
593: GoogleAdsService require a query that
594: specifies the resource to query, the resource attributes and performance metrics
595: to retrieve, the predicates to use for filtering the request, and the segments
596: to use to further break down performance statistics. For more information about
597: query format, see the Google Ads Query Language guide.
598: Retrieve metadata
599: GoogleAdsFieldService retrieves
600: metadata about resources in the Google Ads API, such as the available attributes for a
601: resource and its data type. See the Resource metadata
602: guide for details on querying this service.
603: This service provides information needed in constructing a query to
604: GoogleAdsService. For convenience, the
605: information returned by
606: GoogleAdsFieldService is also available
607: in the fields reference documentation.

427: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets large
428: language models (LLMs) securely interact with external data and applications.
429: The Google Ads MCP server provides a standardized bridge to the Google Ads API. It lets
430: AI agents retrieve and analyze account data, create assets, upload videos, and
431: manage labels by using natural language.
432: Community resources and support
433: GitHub repository: Find demos and examples, report bugs, or suggest
434: features in the google-ads-mcp repository.
435: Use the Issues tab for bug reports and feature requests.
436: Community: Join the #ads-api-ai-tools channel on the Google
437: Advertising Community Discord.
438: Technical overview
439: Integrating the Google Ads MCP server removes the need to write custom code for
440: Google Ads API authentication, resource fetching, data parsing, and supported asset or
441: label mutations. The server exposes callable tools and reference
442: resources (see Core capabilities) that an LLM
443: can inspect and invoke.
444: Key specifications
445: Protocol: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
446: Mode: Read and partial mutate (asset creation, video uploads, and label
447: management with propose-and-confirm validation, or
448: configurable read-only mode)
449: Language: Python 3.10 or later
450: Transport: Standard input/output (stdio) or Streamable HTTP
451: (streamable-http on Cloud Run)
452: Authentication: Application Default Credentials (OAuth 2.0 user
453: credentials or service account) for local stdio, or OAuth 2.0 Web
454: application credentials for remote HTTP
455: Telemetry: Appends google-ads-mcp/VERSION to the x-goog-api-client
456: gRPC request header for usage statistics
457: How the interaction loop works
458: Request: You submit a prompt such as "How is my campaign performance
459: this week?" or "Create a callout asset for our summer sale".
460: Discovery: The LLM inspects its available tools and resources and
461: selects a matching google-ads-mcp tool.
462: Execution or dry-run validation: Read tools query the Google Ads API directly.
463: Mutate tools first run in propose mode (validate_only=True) to validate
464: inputs without committing changes (see Propose-and-confirm safety
465: workflow).
466: Context injection: The MCP server returns structured query results, or
467: proposed change_items entries and a verification checksum digest, to the
468: LLM's context window.
469: Response and confirmation: The LLM presents an answer or asks you to
470: confirm the proposed changes. After you approve, the LLM calls the mutate
471: tool again with validate_only=False and the matching checksum value to
472: commit the change.
473: Get started
474: Follow these steps to configure and run the Google Ads MCP server locally. To deploy
475: a shared remote service instead, see Deployment on Google
476: Cloud.
477: Prerequisites
478: Before you configure the server, complete the following prerequisites in your
479: local environment and the Google Cloud console:
480: Google Cloud project: Create or select a Google Cloud project with the
481: Google Ads API enabled. Enabling the API grants Test access for testing read
482: and mutate workflows against test accounts. To access
483: production accounts, check the Google Ads API overview page for
484: Explorer, Basic, or Standard access, or apply for one of these access
485: levels. Otherwise, production calls fail with an
486: AuthorizationError.CLOUD_PROJECT_NOT_APPROVED_FOR_PRODUCTION error. Google
487: sunset developer tokens (GOOGLE_ADS_DEVELOPER_TOKEN) on
488: September 9, 2026. The Google Cloud project that owns your OAuth client or
489: service account determines your API access level.
490: Credentials: Local stdio mode authenticates with Application Default
491: Credentials (ADC) from an OAuth 2.0 client secret JSON file or a
492: service account in your Cloud project. Set the GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
493: environment variable when needed to specify your default quota or ADC
494: project. Remote streamable-http deployments instead require an OAuth 2.0
495: Web application Client ID and Client secret (see Deploy to Google Cloud
496: Run).
497: Local software (for stdio mode): Install Python 3.10 or
498: later, pipx, and the gcloud command-line
499: tool (used to generate user ADC files).
500: Configuration
501: Generate Application Default Credentials (ADC) using an OAuth
502: client from your API-enabled Google Cloud project and include the Google Ads API
503: scope:
504: gcloud auth application-default login \
505: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
506: --client-id-file=PATH_TO_CLIENT_SECRET_JSON
507: Replace the following:
508: PATH_TO_CLIENT_SECRET_JSON: the path to your OAuth 2.0 client secret
509: JSON file.
510: This command prints Credentials saved to file: [PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON]
511: (such as ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json on Linux
512: and macOS). To authenticate with a service account instead, skip this step
513: and point GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS to your service account key JSON
514: file, or pass --impersonate-service-account to gcloud auth
515: application-default login.
516: Add the server to your host's MCP configuration file (such as
517: ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json, ~/.gemini/settings.json, or
518: ~/.claude/settings.json):
519: {
520: "mcpServers": {
521: "google-ads-mcp": {
522: "command": "pipx",
523: "args": [
524: "run",
525: "--spec",
526: "google-ads-mcp==0.0.6",
527: "google-ads-mcp"
528: ],
529: "env": {
530: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "PROJECT_ID",
531: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON"
532: }
533: }
534: }
535: }
536: Replace the following:
537: PROJECT_ID: your Google Cloud project ID.
538: PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON: the path to the ADC JSON file printed in
539: step 1, or to your service account key JSON file. You can omit
540: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS when using the default gcloud ADC
541: file location.
542: To access client accounts through a manager account, set
543: GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID (10 digits, without hyphens) in env, or
544: pass the login_customer_id parameter on individual tool calls.
545: Tip: For faster startup, install the package once with pipx install
546: google-ads-mcp and set "command": "google-ads-mcp" (with "args": []). When
547: a new Google Ads API version such as v26.2 is released, run pipx upgrade
548: google-ads-mcp (or pipx run --no-cache) to update the bundled google-ads
549: Python client library to 35.x+.
550: Optional: Equip your agent with skills and the Developer Assistant
551: The Google Ads MCP server gives your AI client live access to account reporting
552: data along with asset creation, video upload, and label management tools. Pair
553: the MCP server with the following companion tools to help your agent construct
554: valid Google Ads Query Language (GAQL) queries and diagnose account
555: performance shifts. These tools also generate client library code, such as
556: scripts to link created assets to campaigns or perform other unsupported
557: mutations:
558: Google Ads API AI agent skills: Portable workflow modules (including
559: google-ads-api-mcp-setup, google-ads-api-account-diagnostics, and
560: google-ads-api-quickstart) that help your agent use the Google Ads MCP server
561: with lower token overhead. Run the following command to install them
562: (requires Node.js), or see the Google Ads API AI agent skills
563: guide for Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor setup:
564: npx skills add google/skills/skills/ads
565: Google Ads API Developer Assistant: An open-source plugin (not an officially
566: supported Google product) for Google Antigravity and Claude Code that
567: provides local Protobuf schema inspection, GAQL validation, client library
568: code generation, and offline conversion troubleshooting. See
569: Choose the right Google Ads AI tool or follow the
570: installation guide.
571: Core capabilities
572: The following sections describe the server's read tools, partial mutate tools,
573: and reference resources. Starting in v0.0.6, tools register by default with
574: their category namespace prefix (such as search_search). When upgrading
575: prompts or allowlists from unprefixed releases, update tool names or set an
576: empty prefix ("") in tools_config.yaml (see Configure tool namespaces and
577: read-only mode).
578: Read tools
579: customers_list_accessible_customers (tool
580: list_accessible_customers): Returns the Google Ads customer IDs directly
581: accessible to the authenticated user.
582: search_search (tool search): Builds and runs GAQL
583: SearchStream queries from structured parameters (customer_id,
584: resource, and fields, plus optional conditions, orderings, limit,
585: and login_customer_id) rather than a raw GAQL string. Every query appends
586: PARAMETERS omit_unselected_resource_names=true to fetch resource
587: attributes, metrics, segments, budgets, and status cleanly.
588: metadata_get_resource_metadata (tool get_resource_metadata):
589: Retrieves selectable, filterable, and sortable attributes, metrics, and
590: segments for a Google Ads API resource type (for example, "campaign"). Use this
591: metadata to discover valid query fields—including metrics and segments added
592: in minor releases such as v26.2—before calling the search_search tool.
593: Mutate tools (partial support)
594: assets_create_asset (tool create_asset): Creates standalone Google Ads
595: assets with dedicated parameters for TEXT, IMAGE,
596: YOUTUBE_VIDEO, SITELINK, CALLOUT, and STRUCTURED_SNIPPET asset
597: types. Pass the extra_params dictionary for other mutable AssetService
598: types (such as PRICE, PROMOTION, CALL, or BUSINESS_MESSAGE), and
599: include root-level final_urls alongside sitelink_link_text for
600: SITELINK assets. Local file paths (image_asset_path) work in local
601: stdio mode only. For remote HTTP deployments, pass the base64-encoded
602: image_asset_data parameter with image_asset_mime_type set to
603: IMAGE_PNG, IMAGE_JPEG, or IMAGE_GIF (up to 20 MB).
604: assets_upload_video_asset (tool upload_video_asset): Uploads a
605: local video file (.3gp, .avi, .flv, .mkv, .mov,
606: .mp4, .mpeg, .mpg, .ogg, .webm, or .wmv) to YouTube through the
607: Google Ads API as a FastMCP background task in local stdio mode only. Both
608: video_title and video_description are required parameters. The
609: video_privacy parameter accepts UNLISTED (default) or PUBLIC (allowed
610: only on advertiser-owned brand channels with user OAuth). This tool returns
611: a Google Ads video_upload_id value (and resource name), not the 11-character
612: YouTube video_id. Query you_tube_video_upload with the search_search
613: tool (filtering by you_tube_video_upload.video_upload_id) until
614: you_tube_video_upload.state = 'PROCESSED'. Then pass
615: you_tube_video_upload.video_id as the youtube_video_id parameter to
616: assets_create_asset (asset_type="YOUTUBE_VIDEO").
617: labels_manage_labels (tool manage_labels): Creates, updates, and
618: removes account labels, including name, description, and hex background
619: color.
620: labels_manage_label_associations (tool manage_label_associations):
621: Supports CREATE and REMOVE label association operations (UPDATE is not
622: supported) on CAMPAIGN, CUSTOMER, AD_GROUP, and AD_GROUP_CRITERION
623: resources. For CUSTOMER resources, resource_id is optional and defaults
624: to customer_id. Pass a composite {ad_group_id}~{criterion_id} ID for
625: AD_GROUP_CRITERION resources, and remove associations by passing either
626: resource_id and label_id or association_resource_name. Ad-level
627: AD_GROUP_AD labels are not supported.
628: Note: Mutate support covers standalone asset creation, video uploads, and label
629: management only. The server cannot link assets to campaigns, ad groups, or asset
630: groups, or configure ad-level asset automation settings (such as
631: OVERLAY_TEXT_ON_VIDEOS in v26.2). It also cannot create, modify, pause, or
632: enable campaigns, ad groups, ads, budgets, or bids. For unsupported mutations,
633: pair the server with companion code-generation tools (see Equip your agent with
634: skills and the Developer Assistant).
635: Reference resources
636: The server exposes four read-only MCP resources that remain mounted regardless
637: of your tools_config.yaml settings:
638: resource://discovery-document: JSON REST discovery overview of Google Ads API
639: resources, service methods, and schemas. It complements the
640: metadata_get_resource_metadata tool, which returns selectable, filterable,
641: and sortable GAQL query fields.
642: resource://metrics: HTML reference documentation for Google Ads API metrics.
643: resource://segments: HTML reference documentation for Google Ads API
644: segments.
645: resource://release-notes: HTML Google Ads API release notes covering version
646: changes and new features.
647: Propose-and-confirm safety workflow
648: Every mutate tool (assets_create_asset, assets_upload_video_asset,
649: labels_manage_labels, and labels_manage_label_associations) enforces a
650: two-step propose-and-confirm workflow to help prevent unintended account
651: modifications:
652: Propose (validate_only=True, default): Validates inputs without
653: committing changes. The asset and label tools execute a live Google Ads API
654: validate_only dry run. Because YouTubeVideoUploadService has no dry-run
655: mode, assets_upload_video_asset instead validates the local file and binds
656: its size and modification timestamp. Each tool returns human-readable
657: change_items entries and a stateless SHA-256 checksum digest bound to
658: the customer_id parameter and request payload.
659: Confirm (validate_only=False): After presenting the change_items
660: list and receiving your approval, the agent calls the tool again with
661: validate_only=False, the identical customer_id parameter and arguments,
662: and the checksum value from step 1. The server rejects any missing or
663: mismatched checksum before mutating the account.
664: Note: The checksum value is an unkeyed SHA-256 digest of the request
665: parameters that works statelessly across Cloud Run instances. It prevents
666: accidental parameter drift or local file swaps across turns, but does not
667: replace access control. To hard-block mutations, disable the labels and
668: assets namespaces in tools_config.yaml.
669: Configure tool namespaces and read-only mode
670: The server bundles a default tools_config.yaml file with all five tool
671: categories (customers, search, metadata, labels, and assets) enabled.
672: Customize tools_config.yaml to selectively enable or disable individual tools
673: or namespaces, change or remove namespace prefixes, or enforce a strictly
674: read-only deployment.
675: Important: Whenever namespaces is non-empty, any omitted category is
676: disabled by default, whereas an empty namespaces: {} mapping enables all
677: five categories. Include every category that you want to keep enabled—a file
678: containing only labels: false and assets: false disables the read tools too.
679: At startup, the server resolves tools_config.yaml in the following order:
680: An explicit path in the GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG environment variable
681: (recommended for local stdio hosts, whose working directory can differ
682: from your project folder).
683: A tools_config.yaml file in the server's current working directory.
684: The default tools_config.yaml file bundled with the package.
685: If GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG points to a missing file, or if any resolved
686: configuration file is invalid, the server raises an error at startup instead of
687: falling back to defaults.
688: The following minimal tools_config.yaml file enforces a strictly read-only
689: deployment:
690: namespaces:
691: customers: true
692: search: true
693: metadata: true
694: labels: false
695: assets: false
696: The following tools_config.yaml file customizes prefixes and filters
697: individual tools (for example, exposing the base64 create_asset tool on Cloud
698: Run while disabling the local-only upload_video_asset tool):
699: namespaces:
700: # Default prefix ("customers_list_accessible_customers")
701: customers: true
702: # Empty prefix mounts unprefixed tool names ("search")
703: search: ""
704: # Custom prefix ("schema_get_resource_metadata")
705: metadata: "schema"
706: # Enable only specific tools in a multi-tool category
707: assets:
708: enabled_tools:
709: - create_asset
710: Sample prompts to start
711: Try the following prompts in your MCP client after connecting the server.
712: Ask what the server can do

714: Ask about customers
715: What customers do I have access to?
716: Ask about campaigns
717: How many active campaigns do I have?
718: How is my campaign performance this week?
719: Give me a report of the top spending campaigns split by device category over the last 7 days for account 1234567890

721: Create a callout asset with the text "Free Shipping" for account 1234567890
722: Upload /path/to/promo.mp4 with title "Summer Sale" and description "Summer promo video" for account 1234567890
723: Create a label named "Q4 Promo" with background color #34A853 and apply it to campaign 9876543210 in account 1234567890
724: Note: Video uploads require local stdio mode. Creating a new label and
725: applying it to a campaign runs two sequential propose-and-confirm cycles so the
726: new label_id value can be validated in the association request.
727: Deployment on Google Cloud
728: To share the MCP server across multiple agents or run it as a web service, host
729: it on Google Cloud Run or another cloud infrastructure provider instead of
730: running it locally.
731: Prerequisites
732: A Google Cloud project with the Google Ads API enabled (see
733: Prerequisites for production access requirements).
734: The gcloud command-line tool installed, authenticated, and
735: configured with an active project:
736: gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID
737: Replace the following:
738: PROJECT_ID: your Google Cloud project ID.
739: Build and push a Docker image
740: Use Cloud Build to build and push the container image to Artifact Registry
741: without installing Docker locally:
742: Create a repository in Artifact Registry:
743: gcloud artifacts repositories create mcp-servers \
744: --repository-format=docker --location=us-central1
745: Build and submit the image from a release tag in the GitHub repository (or
746: from . in a local checkout if you customized Dockerfile or
747: tools_config.yaml):
748: gcloud builds submit https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp \
749: --git-source-revision=v0.0.6 \
750: --tag=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/mcp-servers/google-ads-mcp:v0.0.6
751: Replace the following:
752: PROJECT_ID: your Google Cloud project ID.
753: Rebuild and redeploy the image whenever you update google-ads-mcp or
754: upgrade the bundled google-ads Python client library for new Google Ads API
755: releases (such as v26.2).
756: Deploy to Google Cloud Run
757: Configure the following environment variables and secrets for your Cloud Run
758: service:
759: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: The OAuth 2.0 Web application Client
760: ID from your API-enabled Google Cloud project for application-level OAuth
761: authentication. Complete the following OAuth configuration steps:
762: Add the authorized redirect URIs for any AI clients that you plan to
763: connect (such as https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback,
764: https://chatgpt.com/connector_platform_oauth_redirect, or
765: https://antigravity.google/oauth-callback).
766: Add the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords scope to the OAuth
767: consent screen under APIs & Services > OAuth consent screen > Data
768: Access (Add or remove scopes).
769: If your OAuth consent screen publishing status is set to Testing
770: (the default), add the Google Accounts connecting to the MCP server as
771: Test users under APIs & Services > OAuth consent screen >
772: Audience (Test users > + Add users).
773: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: The OAuth Client secret corresponding
774: to your OAuth Client ID.
775: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL: The public base URL of your MCP server (for
776: example, https://google-ads-mcp-xyz-uc.a.run.app). Cloud Run assigns this
777: URL during initial deployment, so deploy without this variable first and
778: update the service afterward.
779: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY (recommended for multi-instance Cloud
780: Run): A persistent secret that signs FastMCP JWTs across container restarts
781: and horizontal scaling.
782: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE (recommended for multi-instance Cloud Run):
783: Backend for OAuth client registrations and tokens. Supported values are
784: redis, firestore, filetree (with GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_PATH for
785: non-Cloud Run VM or mounted-volume deployments), and memory. Setting a
786: backend-specific variable selects that backend even if
787: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE is unset. When all GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_*
788: backend variables are unset, FastMCP uses its default container-local
789: storage; for single-instance testing with local or memory storage, pass
790: --max-instances=1:
791: redis: Set GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_REDIS_URL (defaults to
792: redis://localhost:6379/0) and install py-key-value-aio[redis] in a
793: custom Dockerfile. Redis expires entries automatically.
794: firestore: Optionally set
795: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_PROJECT (defaults to the ADC project)
796: and GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_DATABASE (defaults to
797: (default)). Install .[firestore] in a custom Dockerfile, provision
798: a Firestore database, and grant the roles/datastore.user Identity and
799: Access Management (IAM) role to the Cloud Run service account. The
800: Firestore store filters expired entries on read without deleting them.
801: Because it stores expires_at as a string, Firestore time to live (TTL)
802: policies can't delete expired entries. For long-running deployments,
803: plan periodic cleanup or use Redis.
804: memory: Ephemeral in-memory storage (useful only with
805: --max-instances=1).
806: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY (optional): Dedicated Fernet
807: encryption key (or high-entropy secret) for stored OAuth state. This setting
808: and GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_DISABLE_ENCRYPTION=true apply only when an
809: explicit GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_* backend is configured. If omitted, the
810: server derives an encryption key from GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY, or
811: falls back to GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET when no JWT signing key
812: is set. Setting a dedicated encryption key prevents rotating that fallback
813: secret from invalidating stored OAuth tokens.
814: PORT (optional): Listening port in streamable-http mode (defaults to
815: 8080; Cloud Run sets this automatically).
816: GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID (optional): Default 10-digit manager
817: customer ID (without hyphens) used when tool calls omit the
818: login_customer_id parameter.
819: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG (optional): Container path to a custom
820: tools_config.yaml file (for example, mounted from Secret Manager at
821: /etc/mcp/tools_config.yaml to enforce read-only mode without rebuilding
822: the image). See Configure tool namespaces and read-only
823: mode.
824: Store GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET and GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY
825: in Secret Manager and deploy the service to Google Cloud Run:
826: gcloud run deploy google-ads-mcp \
827: --image=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/mcp-servers/google-ads-mcp:v0.0.6 \
828: --platform=managed \
829: --region=us-central1 \
830: --allow-unauthenticated \
831: --set-env-vars="GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=CLIENT_ID" \
832: --set-secrets="GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET:latest,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY=MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY:latest"
833: After Cloud Run completes the deployment, retrieve the assigned service URL and
834: update the service with the GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL environment variable:
835: gcloud run services update google-ads-mcp \
836: --region=us-central1 \
837: --update-env-vars="GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL=https://CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE_URL"
838: Replace the following:
839: PROJECT_ID: your Google Cloud project ID.
840: CLIENT_ID: your OAuth 2.0 Web application Client ID.
841: MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: the Secret Manager secret name storing your
842: OAuth 2.0 Client secret.
843: MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY: the Secret Manager secret name storing your JWT
844: signing key.
845: CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE_URL: the hostname assigned to your Cloud Run service
846: (for example, google-ads-mcp-xyz-uc.a.run.app).
847: Authentication and security model
848: Deploying with --allow-unauthenticated disables Cloud Run's infrastructure IAM
849: check (roles/run.invoker) so external AI clients can connect without Google
850: Cloud service account tokens. Authentication is delegated to the application
851: layer instead:
852: When GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and
853: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET are set, the server enforces Google
854: OAuth 2.0 on every request and returns a 401 Unauthorized HTTP status code
855: to unauthenticated callers. Every tool call executes under the authenticated
856: caller's OAuth identity.
857: Omitting --allow-unauthenticated requires callers to pass Google Cloud
858: OIDC identity tokens with every request. Standard AI clients (such as Claude
859: and ChatGPT) use end-user OAuth rather than Google Cloud IAM tokens, so
860: direct connections require --allow-unauthenticated paired with
861: application-level OAuth.
862: Caution: Never omit GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and
863: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET when deploying with
864: --allow-unauthenticated. Those environment variables switch the server from
865: local stdio mode to streamable-http transport. Without them, the server
866: falls back to Application Default Credentials (ADC) and exposes the container's
867: service account credentials to unauthenticated callers.
868: Configure the MCP client
869: After deployment, configure your MCP client with the Cloud Run service URL.
870: Because the server enforces OAuth 2.0, your client must support the MCP OAuth
871: flow or supply an authorized Bearer token:
872: OAuth-enabled clients: In clients that support MCP OAuth discovery (such
873: as Antigravity), connecting triggers a Google sign-in prompt to grant the
874: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords scope (shown as .../auth/adwords
875: in the Google Cloud console).
876: Third-party AI platforms (Claude, ChatGPT): In your client's connector
877: settings, add a custom connector pointing to your service URL with the
878: /mcp path (for example, https://google-ads-mcp-xyz-uc.a.run.app/mcp).
879: Select OAuth 2.0 authentication with your OAuth Client ID and Client secret,
880: and confirm that the client's callback URI is in your OAuth client's
881: authorized redirect URIs.
882: Clients without OAuth support: Clients that don't support HTTP OAuth
883: flows receive a 401 Unauthorized HTTP status code. For those clients, use
884: the local stdio configuration instead.
885: The following example configures the gemini command-line tool in
886: ~/.gemini/settings.json (for Google Antigravity in
887: ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json, replace "httpUrl" with "serverUrl" or
888: "url"):
889: {
890: "mcpServers": {
891: "google-ads-mcp": {
892: "httpUrl": "https://CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE_URL/mcp"
893: }
894: }
895: }
896: Replace the following:
897: CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE_URL: the hostname assigned to your Cloud Run service
898: (for example, google-ads-mcp-xyz-uc.a.run.app).
899: Next steps
900: Install Google Ads API AI agent skills
901: Compare Google Ads AI tools and the Google Ads API Developer Assistant

1: # Google Ads MCP Server
2: An [MCP (Model Context Protocol)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that enables LLMs and AI agents to query and manage [Google Ads](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api) accounts.
3: ## Table of Contents
4: - [Overview](#overview)
5: - [Quickstart & Setup](#quickstart--setup)
6: - [1. Prerequisites](#1-prerequisites)
7: - [2. Choose an Authentication Mode](#2-choose-an-authentication-mode)
8: - [3. Configure Your MCP Client](#3-configure-your-mcp-client)
9: - [Tools & Resources](#tools--resources)
10: - [Available Tools](#available-tools)
11: - [Available Resources](#available-resources)
12: - [Configuration & Security](#configuration--security)
13: - [Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow](#propose--confirm-safety-workflow)
14: - [Configuring and Namespacing Tools](#configuring-and-namespacing-tools)
15: - [Tool Call Auditability](#tool-call-auditability)
16: - [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)
17: - [Deployment](#deployment)
18: - [Local Container Deployment (Docker / Podman)](#local-container-deployment-docker--podman)
19: - [Google Cloud Run Deployment](#google-cloud-run-deployment)
20: - [Try It Out](#try-it-out)
21: - [Contributing](#contributing)
22: ## Overview
23: The Google Ads MCP Server exposes [MCP Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/tools) and [MCP Resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/resources) backed by the [Google Ads API](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/reference/rpc/latest/overview). It supports:
24: - **Read & reporting workflows**: GAQL queries, accessible customer discovery, resource field metadata, and API reference resources.
25: - **Guarded account mutations**: Asset creation, video uploads, and label management protected by a two-step **Propose & Confirm** workflow.
26: - **Flexible deployment**: Run locally over `stdio` with Application Default Credentials, or over **Streamable HTTP** with FastMCP's OAuth proxy and structured audit logging.
27: > **Notes:**
28: > - Connecting an LLM or agent to this server exposes your accessible Google Ads account data to that client.
29: > - API calls made by this server include an MCP telemetry header used by Google to collect usage statistics and improve the product.
30: > - Report bugs or feature requests on the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp/issues).
31: ---
32: ## Quickstart & Setup
33: ### 1. Prerequisites
34: 1. **Python & `pipx`** (for local non-container setups): Python 3.11+ and [`pipx`](https://pipx.pypa.io/stable/#install-pipx).
35: To run a specific released version from PyPI:
36: ```shell
37: pipx run --spec "google-ads-mcp==X.Y.Z" google-ads-mcp
38: ```
39: 2. **Google Cloud Project**: Enable the [Google Ads API](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/googleads.googleapis.com) in your Google Cloud project ([how to enable APIs](https://support.google.com/googleapi/answer/6158841)).
40: ### 2. Choose an Authentication Mode
41: The server supports two authentication and transport modes out of the box:
42: | Mode | Transport | Best For |
43: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
44: | **Mode A: Application Default Credentials (ADC)** | `stdio` | Single-user local CLI/IDE agents where the MCP client spawns the server directly. |
45: | **Mode B: FastMCP OAuth Proxy** | `streamable-http` | Shared/remote deployments or local containers where server credentials stay isolated from MCP client configs. |
46: #### Mode A: Local `stdio` with Application Default Credentials (ADC)
47: Configure [Application Default Credentials (ADC)](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/provide-credentials-adc) for a user or service account with access to your Google Ads accounts. Credentials must include the Google Ads API scope (`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords`). See [Manage OAuth Clients](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549257) if you need to create an OAuth desktop or web client first.
48: - **Option 1 — User credentials with an OAuth client JSON file:**
49: ```shell
50: gcloud auth application-default login \
51: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
52: --client-id-file=YOUR_CLIENT_JSON_FILE
53: ```
54: - **Option 2 — Service account impersonation:**
55: ```shell
56: gcloud auth application-default login \
57: --impersonate-service-account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL \
58: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
59: ```
60: When the command finishes, note the credentials path printed to the console (`Credentials saved to file: [PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON]`) for your MCP client configuration.
61: #### Mode B: Streamable HTTP with FastMCP OAuth Proxy
62: Setting `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` enables FastMCP's [OAuth proxy](https://gofastmcp.com/servers/auth/oauth-proxy) for dynamic per-user Google OAuth login and automatically switches the server transport from `stdio` to `streamable-http` (default endpoint: `http://localhost:8080/mcp`).
63: Run the server as a standalone process or container (see [Deployment](#deployment) and [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)), then point your MCP client at the HTTP endpoint—no server secrets are stored in client configs.
64: ### 3. Configure Your MCP Client
65: #### Connecting via Streamable HTTP (Mode B — Recommended for Shared or Container Setups)
66: - **Antigravity / Antigravity IDE** ([MCP setup docs](https://antigravity.google/docs/mcp)):
67: Use `serverUrl` (required for Streamable HTTP in current Antigravity releases; do not use `httpUrl`):
68: ```json
69: {
70: "mcpServers": {
71: "google-ads-mcp": {
72: "serverUrl": "http://localhost:8080/mcp"
73: }
74: }
75: }
76: ```
77: - **Codex CLI** ([Codex MCP docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp/)):
78: ```shell
79: codex mcp add google_ads --url http://localhost:8080/mcp
80: codex mcp login google_ads
81: ```
82: #### Spawning Locally via `stdio` + ADC (Mode A)
83: Add the following `mcpServers` block to your client configuration, replacing `PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON` and `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` ([how to find your project ID](https://support.google.com/googleapi/answer/7014113)):
84: ```json
85: {
86: "mcpServers": {
87: "google-ads-mcp": {
88: "command": "pipx",
89: "args": [
90: "run",
91: "--spec",
92: "git+https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp.git",
93: "google-ads-mcp"
94: ],
95: "env": {
96: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON",
97: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
98: }
99: }
100: }
101: }
102: ```
103: > **Tip:** To pin a published PyPI release instead of tracking `main`, change `"git+https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp.git"` to `"google-ads-mcp==X.Y.Z"`. Note that `stdio` mode stores the ADC file path in the client's config; prefer [Local Container Deployment](#local-container-deployment-docker--podman) if client configs are shared or synced across tools.
104: #### Manager Accounts (`login_customer_id`)
105: If you access client accounts through a Google Ads Manager Account (MCC), you can either:
106: 1. Pass `login_customer_id` per tool call (takes precedence when provided), or
107: 2. Set `GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID` in the server's `env` configuration as a default:
108: ```json
109: "env": {
110: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON",
111: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
112: "GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID": "YOUR_MANAGER_CUSTOMER_ID"
113: }
114: ```
115: See [Google Ads API Call Structure (`login-customer-id`)](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/concepts/call-structure#cid) for details.
116: #### Other MCP Clients (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code)
117: The `mcpServers` JSON format works across standard MCP clients—place it in the client's configuration file (for example, `~/.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code, `.cursor/mcp.json` for Cursor, or `.vscode/mcp.json` for VS Code).
118: ---
119: ## Tools & Resources
120: ### Available Tools
121: By default, tools are mounted with their category namespace prefix (`<namespace>_<tool>`). Namespaces and individual tools can be customized via `tools_config.yaml` (see [Configuring and Namespacing Tools](#configuring-and-namespacing-tools)).
122: | Default Tool Name | Namespace | Type | Description |
123: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
124: | `search_search` | `search` | Read | Queries Google Ads account data using GAQL (Google Ads Query Language). |
125: | `metadata_get_resource_metadata` | `metadata` | Read | Retrieves selectable, filterable, and sortable field metadata for a Google Ads API resource (e.g., `campaign`). |
126: | `customers_list_accessible_customers` | `customers` | Read | Lists customer IDs directly accessible to the authenticated user. |
127: | `assets_create_asset` | `assets` | Mutate | Creates Google Ads assets (`TEXT`, `IMAGE`, `YOUTUBE_VIDEO`, `SITELINK`, `CALLOUT`, `STRUCTURED_SNIPPET`, plus additional types via `extra_params`). Note: `image_asset_path` is local `stdio` only; use base64 `image_asset_data` over HTTP. |
128: | `assets_upload_video_asset` | `assets` | Mutate | Uploads a local video file to YouTube via a background task so it can be referenced by video assets (local `stdio` mode only). |
129: | `labels_manage_labels` | `labels` | Mutate | Creates, updates, and removes account labels. |
130: | `labels_manage_label_associations` | `labels` | Mutate | Creates and removes label associations on `CAMPAIGN`, `CUSTOMER`, `AD_GROUP`, and `AD_GROUP_CRITERION` resources. |
131: ### Available Resources
132: | Resource URI | Description |
133: | :--- | :--- |
134: | `resource://discovery-document` | Google Ads API REST discovery document describing the API surface, resources, methods, and schemas. (Prefer `metadata_get_resource_metadata` when looking up specific queryable GAQL fields.) |
135: | `resource://metrics` | Reference documentation for reporting metrics in the Google Ads API. |
136: | `resource://segments` | Reference documentation for reporting segments in the Google Ads API. |
137: | `resource://release-notes` | Release notes for the latest version of the Google Ads API. |
138: ---
139: ## Configuration & Security
140: ### Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow
141: All mutate tools (`assets_create_asset`, `assets_upload_video_asset`, `labels_manage_labels`, and `labels_manage_label_associations`) enforce a mandatory two-step safety workflow:
142: 1. **Propose (`validate_only=True`, default)**: Validates the operation (including a Google Ads API `validate_only` dry run where supported) without committing changes. Returns human-readable `change_items` and a cryptographic `checksum` bound to the `customer_id` and parameters.
143: 2. **Confirm (`validate_only=False`)**: After explicit user approval, pass the exact same parameters and `customer_id` along with the `checksum` from step 1. Missing or mismatched checksums are rejected before mutating the account.
144: ### Configuring and Namespacing Tools
145: Use `tools_config.yaml` to selectively enable or disable tool categories/tools and customize namespace prefixes. A default configuration with all categories enabled is bundled with the package.
146: The server resolves `tools_config.yaml` in the following order:
147: 1. Path specified by `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG`.
148: 2. `./tools_config.yaml` in the current working directory.
149: 3. The default `tools_config.yaml` bundled with the package.
150: If an explicitly configured file is missing or any resolved file is invalid, startup fails immediately.
151: ```yaml
152: namespaces:
153: # Enable category with default prefix -> "customers_list_accessible_customers"
154: customers: true
155: # Enable category with custom prefix -> "query_search"
156: search: "query"
157: # Fine-grained control over individual tools in a category
158: metadata:
159: enabled: true
160: prefix: "metadata"
161: enabled_tools:
162: - get_resource_metadata: true
163: # Disable mutate categories for a strictly read-only deployment
164: labels: false
165: assets: false
166: ```
167: ### Tool Call Auditability
168: Every tool invocation—including background worker runs via `TasksExtension`—is recorded by `AuditMiddleware`, which emits structured JSON events (`"tool_call"` and `"task_execution"`) to the `ads_mcp.audit` logger:
169: - **Actor (`actor`)**: Authentication mode (`oauth` or `adc`), opaque OAuth identifiers (`sub`, `client_id`, `scopes`), MCP `session_id` (per-request on sessionless MCP `2026-07-28` connections), and MCP `client_info`. Raw PII such as `email` and `name` is omitted.
170: - **Execution context**: Unique `audit_id`, tool name, MCP `call_id` (and `task_id` for background tasks), `received_at` UTC timestamp, `customer_id`, `login_customer_id`, `mutation_phase` (`READ`, `PROPOSE`, or `COMMIT`), `checksum`, `schema_hash`, `status` (`completed`, `empty`, `enqueued`, `error`, or `failed`), and `duration_ms`.
171: - **Redacted arguments**: `arguments` with binary/base64 media payloads and Google Ads sensitive/PII fields (in both `snake_case` and protobuf JSON `camelCase`) replaced with `REDACTED`.
172: Audit records can also be persisted to `filetree`, `redis`, `firestore`, or `memory` via the `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_*` variables below. Stored records remain unencrypted redacted JSON by default so backends like Firestore stay queryable across OAuth secret rotations; set `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to enable Fernet encryption with a dedicated HKDF salt isolated from OAuth token storage.
173: ### Environment Variables Reference
174: #### Core & OAuth Proxy
175: | Variable | Description |
176: | :--- | :--- |
177: | `GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID` | Optional default Manager Account (MCC) customer ID when accessing client accounts through a manager. |
178: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG` | Optional path to a custom `tools_config.yaml` file. |
179: | `PORT` | HTTP listen port when running in Streamable HTTP mode (default: `8080`). |
180: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Google Cloud OAuth 2.0 Client ID. Setting both ID and Secret enables OAuth Proxy & Streamable HTTP mode. |
181: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Google Cloud OAuth 2.0 Client Secret. |
182: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL` | Public base URL of the HTTP server (default: `http://localhost:8080`). |
183: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY` | Recommended for multi-instance or persistent HTTP deployments to sign FastMCP JWTs consistently. |
184: #### OAuth State & Audit Persistence
185: Both OAuth state storage (`GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_*`) and optional audit record storage (`GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_*`) support `filetree`, `redis`, `firestore`, and `memory` backends.
186: > **Optional backend extras:** Install `pip install "py-key-value-aio[redis]"` for Redis or `pip install "google-ads-mcp[firestore]"` for Firestore.
187: | OAuth Storage Variable | Audit Storage Equivalent | Description |
188: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
189: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_TYPE` | Backend type: `filetree`, `redis`, `firestore`, or `memory`. |
190: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_PATH` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_PATH` | Directory path when using the `filetree` backend. |
191: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_REDIS_URL` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_REDIS_URL` | Redis connection URL (defaults to `redis://localhost:6379/0`). |
192: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_PROJECT` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_PROJECT` | GCP project for `firestore` (defaults to ADC project; setting this implicitly selects `firestore`). |
193: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_DATABASE` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_DATABASE` | Firestore database name (defaults to `(default)`). |
194: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Fernet key (or secret material) for encrypting stored records. OAuth storage falls back to JWT/OAuth secret; audit storage is unencrypted unless explicitly set. |
195: | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_DISABLE_ENCRYPTION` | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_DISABLE_ENCRYPTION` | Set to `true` to disable storage encryption. |
196: | — | `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_AUDIT_STORAGE_TTL_SECONDS` | Optional retention TTL (in positive seconds) for persisted audit records. |
197: ---
198: ## Deployment
199: Remote and containerized deployments run in Streamable HTTP mode using the FastMCP OAuth Proxy (`GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`).
200: ### Local Container Deployment (Docker / Podman)
201: Running the server in a local rootless container isolates OAuth secrets and storage encryption keys from MCP client configurations.
202: 1. **Build the image:**
203: ```shell
204: docker build --tag google-ads-mcp:latest .
205: # or with Podman:
206: podman build --tag localhost/google-ads-mcp:latest --file Dockerfile .
207: ```
208: 2. **Run with isolated secrets and persistent OAuth state:**
209: Keep your `.env` file outside the repository with owner-only permissions, bind port `8080` strictly to `127.0.0.1` for local agents, and mount a dedicated volume for `filetree` OAuth state (`GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_PATH=/var/lib/google-ads-mcp`):
210: ```shell
211: docker run -d --name google-ads-mcp \
212: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
213: --env-file /absolute/host/path/google-ads-mcp.env \
214: -v google-ads-mcp-oauth:/var/lib/google-ads-mcp:rw \
215: --read-only --security-opt no-new-privileges --cap-drop ALL \
216: google-ads-mcp:latest
217: ```
218: For systemd/Podman Quadlet setups, the equivalent `.container` unit is:
219: ```ini
220: [Container]
221: Image=localhost/google-ads-mcp:latest
222: PublishPort=127.0.0.1:8080:8080
223: EnvironmentFile=/absolute/host/path/google-ads-mcp.env
224: Volume=google-ads-mcp-oauth.volume:/var/lib/google-ads-mcp:rw
225: ReadOnly=true
226: NoNewPrivileges=true
227: DropCapability=all
228: ```
229: #### HTTP Interoperability Notes
230: - **Stateful Streamable HTTP**: Keep stateful Streamable HTTP enabled (the default). It serves both MCP 2025 clients (`Mcp-Session-Id` + `GET` SSE) and MCP 2026 clients (sessionless `POST` + `subscriptions/listen`). Do not enable FastMCP's `stateless_http` option on a shared endpoint, as it removes the legacy `GET` SSE channel.
231: - **FastMCP 4 & OAuth callback compatibility**: The server targets `fastmcp>=4.0.6,<5` and `mcp[cli]>=2.0.0,<3`. The `Dockerfile` applies a version-guarded patch that stops advertising RFC 9207 `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported` as mandatory for compatibility with Codex CLI OAuth callbacks, failing the build loudly if the upstream FastMCP target changes.
232: ### Google Cloud Run Deployment
233: #### Prerequisites
234: 1. A Google Cloud project with billing enabled.
235: 2. The `gcloud` CLI authenticated and configured:
236: ```shell
237: gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
238: ```
239: #### Step 1: Build and Push the Container Image
240: Create an Artifact Registry repository and build with Cloud Build (no local Docker required):
241: ```shell
242: gcloud artifacts repositories create mcp-servers \
243: --repository-format=docker \
244: --location=us-central1
245: gcloud builds submit \
246: --tag us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/mcp-servers/google-ads-mcp:latest .
247: ```
248: > **Using Firestore for persistent OAuth/audit storage on Cloud Run:**
249: > 1. Install the Firestore extra in your `Dockerfile` (`RUN uv pip install --system ".[firestore]"`).
250: > 2. Provision a Firestore database in your GCP project and grant the Cloud Run service account `roles/datastore.user`.
251: > 3. Note that `py-key-value-aio`'s Firestore store filters expired entries on read without deleting them (and writes `expires_at` as a string rather than a native timestamp), so plan a periodic cleanup job for long-running deployments—or use Redis (`GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE=redis`), which expires keys natively.
252: #### Step 2: Deploy to Cloud Run
253: Deploy the service with your OAuth credentials, persistent JWT signing key, and storage backend. On first deploy, you can omit `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL` until Cloud Run assigns your service URL, then update it:
254: ```shell
255: gcloud run deploy google-ads-mcp \
256: --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/mcp-servers/google-ads-mcp:latest \
257: --platform managed \
258: --region us-central1 \
259: --allow-unauthenticated \
260: --set-env-vars="GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=YOUR_PROJECT_ID,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=YOUR_CLIENT_ID,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL=https://your-cloud-run-url.a.run.app,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY=YOUR_JWT_SIGNING_KEY,GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE=firestore"
261: ```
262: Add `GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID=YOUR_MANAGER_CUSTOMER_ID` to `--set-env-vars` if your accounts are accessed via a manager account.
263: #### Step 3: Connect Your MCP Client
264: Point your MCP client at the Cloud Run `/mcp` endpoint:
265: ```json
266: {
267: "mcpServers": {
268: "google-ads-mcp": {
269: "serverUrl": "https://your-cloud-run-url.a.run.app/mcp"
270: }
271: }
272: }
273: ```
274: ---
275: ## Try It Out
276: Launch your MCP client and verify that `google-ads-mcp` appears in the connected servers list. Try prompts such as:
277: - `What can the google-ads-mcp server do?`
278: - `What customers do I have access to?`
279: - `How many active campaigns do I have for customer ID 1234567890?`
280: - `How is my campaign performance this week for customer ID 1234567890?`
281: > **Tip:** Most tools require a `customer_id`. Including the customer ID directly in your prompt makes switching across multiple accounts faster.
282: ---
283: ## Contributing
284: Contributions are welcome! See the [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) to get started.
285: Project maintainers can find the Trusted Publishing and release workflow in the [Release Guide](docs/releasing.md).

sources.numbered_text:
1: # Marketing API overview
2: Use the Marketing API to automate advertising across Meta technologies. The API provides functions for ad creation, management, and performance analysis.
3: You can programmatically generate ad campaigns, ad sets, and individual ads, deploying and adjusting them based on real-time performance data. Automated ad creation also lets businesses reach larger audiences while using fewer resources.
4: In addition to ad creation, you can:
5: * Update, pause, or delete ads
6: * Ensure that campaigns remain aligned with business objectives
7: * Access detailed insights and analytics to track ad performance and make data-driven decisions to improve outcomes
8: ## How it works
9: ### Ad campaigns
10: A campaign is the highest-level organizational structure within an ad account and should represent a single objective, for example, to drive Page post engagement. Setting the objective of the campaign enforces validation on any ads you add to that campaign to ensure they also have the correct objective.
11: ### Ad sets
12: Ad sets are groups of ads that configure the budget and period the ads should run for. The budget, billing, and duration are set at the ad set level and apply to all ads in the set. All ads contained within an ad set should also have the same targeting and optimization goal.
13: Create an ad set for each target audience with your bid; ads in the set target the same audience with the same bid. Creating one ad set per audience helps control the amount you spend on each audience and determine when the audience will see your ads. It also provides metrics for each audience.
14: ### Ad creatives
15: Ad creatives contain only the visual elements of the ad, and you can't change them once they're created. Each ad account has a creative library to store creatives for reuse in ads.
16: ### Ads
17: An ad object contains all the information necessary to display an ad on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and WhatsApp, including the ad creative. Create multiple ads in each ad set to optimize ad delivery based on different images, links, video, text, or placements.
18: ### Ad components
19: The following table shows how Marketing API ad components map to ad campaigns, ad sets, and ads.
20: | Component | Ad Campaign | Ad Set | Ad |
21: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
22: | **Objective** | ✓ | | |
23: | **Schedule** | | ✓ | |
24: | **Budget** | | ✓ | |
25: | **Bidding** | | ✓ | |
26: | **Audience** | | ✓ | |
27: | **Ad Creative** | | | ✓ |
28: ---
29: Full documentation index for this product: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/llms.txt
