25: Summarize this article for me
26: In this article
27: The LinkedIn API uses OAuth 2.0 for member (user) authorization and API authentication. Applications must be authorized and authenticated before they can fetch data from LinkedIn or get access to LinkedIn member data.
28: There are two types of Authorization Flows available:
29: Member Authorization (3-legged OAuth)
30: Application Authorization (2-legged OAuth)
31: Depending on the type of permissions your integration will require, follow one of the authorization flows to get started.
32: Note
33: There are several third-party libraries in the open source community which abstract the OAuth 2.0 authentication process in every major programming language.
34: LinkedIn does not support TLS 1.0.
35: Member Authorization (3-legged OAuth Flow)
36: The Member Authorization grants permissions to your application by a LinkedIn member to access the member’s resources on LinkedIn. Your application has no access to these resources without member approval. The Member Auth uses the 3-legged OAuth code flow. For step-by-step instructions on how to implement 3-legged OAuth, see Authorization Code Flow (3-legged OAuth) page.
37: Tip
38: When to use 3-legged OAuth
39: Use this flow if you are requesting access to a member's account to use their data and make requests on their behalf. This is the most commonly used permission type across LinkedIn APIs. Open permissions available to all applications are of this type such as r_liteprofile, r_emailaddress, and w_member_social.
40: Member Auth Permissions
41: Member Authorization Permissions are granted by a LinkedIn member to access members resources on LinkedIn. Permissions are authorization consents to access LinkedIn resources. The LinkedIn platform uses permissions to protect and prevent abuse of member data. Your application must have the appropriate permissions before it can access data. To see the list of permissions, descriptions and access details, refer to Getting Access to LinkedIn APIs page.
42: Application Authorization (2-legged OAuth Client Credential Flow)
43: Application Authorization or using 2-Legged OAuth grants permissions to your application to access protected LinkedIn resources. If you are accessing APIs that are not member specific, use this flow. Not all APIs support Application Authorization. For example, Marketing APIs you must use Member Authorization explained above. For step-by-step instructions on how to implement 2-legged OAuth, see Client Credential Flow (2-legged OAuth) page.
44: Note
45: Always request the minimal permission scopes necessary for your use case.
46: Application Auth Permissions
47: Application Authorization Permissions are granted to applications to access LinkedIn protected resources. To see the list of permissions, descriptions and access details, refer to Getting Access to LinkedIn APIs page.
48: Sample Application
49: You can explore the OAuth Sample Applications that enables you to try out RESTful OAuth calls to the LinkedIn Authentication server. The sample app is available in Java.
50: Additionally, you can also explore the Marketing Sample Application.

27: Warning
28: Deprecation Notice:
29: The Marketing Version 202601 (Marketing January 2026) will be sunset on January 15, 2027. We recommend that you migrate to the latest versioned APIs to avoid disruptions. For information on all the supported versions, refer to the migrations documentation.
30: If you haven’t yet migrated and have questions, submit a request on the LinkedIn Developer Support Portal.
31: Campaigns define the ad schedule and budget (daily or total). A campaign can have a specific start and end date or run continuously until the budget is spent. Campaigns can target a specific audience based on categories such as job title, job function, and seniority.
32: Limitations
33: AD ACCOUNTS
34: Limited to 5,000 campaigns (regardless of campaign status).
35: Maximum of 1,000 concurrent campaigns in ACTIVE status at any given time.
36: CAMPAIGNS
37: Maximum of 15 active creatives and 85 inactive creatives.
38: Active until it reaches its end time or gets deleted.
39: Paused campaigns are considered active until their designated end times.
40: CREATIVES
41: Creatives must match the ad format selected during campaign creation.
42: If no Ad format is set, it's set by the first creative created under that campaign.
43: Dynamic, Carousel, and Video Ad Campaigns must have their format set during creation.
44: Permissions
45: The following conditions should be met for successful Ad Account User API calls:
46: Scope permission accessibility for:
47: rw_ads (read/write).
48: r_ads (read-only).
49: The Ad Account user that assigns permissions has one of the following roles:
50: ACCOUNT_BILLING_ADMIN.
51: ACCOUNT_MANAGER.
52: CAMPAIGN_MANAGER.
53: CREATIVE_MANAGER.
54: VIEWER (read-only, even with rw_ads scope).
55: For more information on Ad Account roles and permissions:
56: Ad Account User Role Definitions.
57: Create and Manage Ad Account Users.
58: Campaign Types
59: The following ad placements or Campaign Types are available on LinkedIn:
60: Campaign Type
61: Description
62: Best Practices
63: TEXT_AD
64: Text ads include a headline, brief text, and an image. They can be placed at the top of the page or on the right rail of a variety of LinkedIn desktop pages.
65: Text Ads
66: SPONSORED_UPDATES
67: Sponsored Content: The Sponsored Content campaign in Campaign Manager. Provides the option to browse existing content to select campaign.
68: Sponsored Updates
69: SPONSORED_INMAILS
70: Sponsored Messaging: These ads are displayed via desktop and mobile when members are active anywhere on LinkedIn.
71: Sponsored Inmails
72: DYNAMIC
73: Personalized ads that are automatically populated with a members' profile photo and other data dynamically pulled from their LinkedIn profiles. APIs are available for self-service campaign formats such as Follower Ads, Spotlight Ads, and Jobs Ads.
74: Dynamic ads
75: EVENT AD
76: LinkedIn Event Ads are a type of Sponsored Content that allow advertisers to promote events directly in the LinkedIn feed. This ad type allows advertisers to seamlessly promote a LinkedIn event to a defined audience before, during, and after the event.
77: CONTENT
78: This format is only available for managed accounts and cannot be managed through the API or Campaign Manager.
79: For more information, refer to Campaign Objective API Mapping.
80: Direct Sponsored Content
81: Direct Sponsored Content (DSC) is a sponsored update that doesn't appear on the organization page. It allows your organization to personalize, test, and refine its messages to improve content quality for a targeted audience without cluttering the organization page.
82: Direct Sponsored Content can be created by:
83: Ad Account Users with permission scope r_ads or rw_ads with a role higher than VIEWER.
84: Organization users with DIRECT_SPONSORED_CONTENT_POSTER or ADMINISTRATOR roles.

450: Frequency Optimization Preference
451: Currently, only the BRAND_AWARENESS objective type supports this field for frequency cap management. If a frequency cap is not set, LinkedIn will dynamically apply a cap to optimize your selected optimization target.
452: Note
453: Frequency cap management is currently fully available on Connected TV (CTV) only campaigns. We are gradually releasing to the other Brand Awareness campaigns, and you might not have access to it at this time.
454: Ad Frequency and Frequency Cap
455: Ad frequency is crucial for building long-term memory and brand awareness with your target audience. Frequency refers to the number of times a member account has been shown your ad campaign within a specific time period. Currently, we support a 7-day span and the MAX_FREQUENCY optimization type, which allows you to customize your campaign-level frequency cap.
456: A frequency cap sets an upper limit on the number of times an ad in your campaign will be shown to a single member account within a 7-day period. Set the frequency cap to any number between 3 and 30 impressions during this time.

590: Budgeting
591: The following options are available for budgeting at the campaign level:
592: dailyBudget - Campaigns run until the daily ad spend for the campaign has reached the daily budget limit. At midnight UTC, the daily budget resets and the campaign continues to run the next day.
593: totalBudget - Campaigns run until the total ad spend for the life of the campaign has reached the total budget limit. Deprecated for campaigns not using lifetime pacing.
594: If both daily budget and total budget are set for the campaign, the campaign runs until the ad spend has either reached daily spend limit and/or the total spend limit.
595: Dynamic Ads campaigns must set both daily and total budgets.
596: Targeting Discrimination Notice
597: Applications utilizing LinkedIn's targeting capabilities are required to display a notice in their user interface notifying advertisers that they can't use LinkedIn to discriminate against members based on personal characteristics. The notice should include the following text:
598: "LinkedIn tools may not be used to discriminate based on personal characteristics such as gender, age, race, or ethnicity.Learn more."
599: Lifetime Pacing
600: Lifetime Pacing provides advertisers a budget option that enables running a campaign according to a projected budget based on the predicted spend curve throughout the campaign's lifetime. Creating a spending strategy in this manner optimizes advertiser return on investment (ROI) value.
601: As an example, advertisers can simply set a lifetime budget of $10,000, and run a campaign for one month. With Lifetime Pacing, LinkedIn's delivery system can figure out how to spend the budget efficiently based on the supply curve during the allocated month time period. To illustrate this efficiency, the campaign would spend less on a Saturday when fewer LinkedIn member use the site, but more on a Monday when more members are viewing the site.
602: While the lifetime budget is a new spending option, we permit advertisers to use other budget options including the "set daily budget alone" or "set both daily budget and lifetime budget" to accommodate their different requirements.
603: Benefits of Lifetime Pacing
604: For all LinkedIn advertisers, Lifetime Pacing delivers the lifetime budget throughout the campaign lifetime to improve advertiser ROI, stabilize the cost per result value, and simplify campaign creation and optimization by leveraging advanced pacing, forecasting, and machine learning techniques.
605: To enable Lifetime Pacing, set the pacingStrategy to LIFETIME.
606: The four strategies one can use are a daily budget with:
607: A continuous schedule.
608: A fixed schedule.
609: A total budget with a fixed schedule.
610: A total budget with continuous schedule.
611: Use a Daily Budget with a Continuous Schedule
612: To use this option, set dailyBudget and runSchedule.start. By using a daily budget with a continuous schedule, the advantage is you have great spend control while running a non-stop campaign. In this approach, LinkedIn can charge you up to 150% of your daily budget if there’re great opportunities in the auction for you on a single day.
613: Use a Daily Budget with a Fixed Schedule
614: To use this option, set dailyBudget, runSchedule.start and runSchedule.end. By using a daily budget with a fixed schedule that has an explicit end date, the advantage is Lifetime Pacing will pace your lifetime budget (daily budget X days of the campaign flight time) in order to get the optimal ROI for you. In this approach, LinkedIn can charge you up to 150% of your daily budget if there’re great opportunities in the auction for you on a single day. Also, this approach spends in total no more than an amount equal to the following value: (the total number of days of the campaign flight time X the daily budget).
615: Use a Total Budget with a Fixed Schedule
616: To use this option, set totalBudget, runSchedule.start and runSchedule.end. By using a total budget with a fixed schedule that has a specific end date for spending, the advantage is Lifetime Pacing will pace your lifetime budget to obtain optimal results. In this approach, you spend no more than the full budget for the lifetime of the campaign. LinkedIn applies the budget optimally through the campaign lifetime up to the specified final day to maximize ROI.
617: Use a Daily Budget and a Total Budget with a Continuous Schedule
618: To use this option, set dailyBudget, totalBudget and runSchedule.start. By using a daily budget and a total budget with a continuous schedule without an end date, the advantage is that you have the maximum control of your spending for both the daily and lifetime budget approaches.
619: In this approach, LinkedIn can charge you up to 150% of your daily budget if there are strong opportunities in the auction for you on a given day. This approach ensures that total spend does not exceed the specified budget. The campaign stops when the budget is depleted.
620: Optimization of Campaigns
621: optimizationTargetType is used to optimize spending for a campaign. Depending on what value is populated in this field, the campaign enables either auto, manual, target cost, or cost cap bidding.
622: For auto-bidding campaigns created using legacy Objectives, the costType is always CPM. The unitCost defaults to 0. Note that there are no validations and can be set to any arbitrary high/low value.
623: If optimizationTargetType is switched to a manual bidding, target cost, or cost cap bidding type, unitCost should be set to a non-negative value appropriate to the dailyBudget. For manual bidding, target cost, or cost cap bidding types, if unitCost is 0, the campaign does not deliver.
624: Warning
625: Failure to set the unitCost correctly can lead to unexpected expenses.
626: We recommend updating both unitCost and optimizationTargetType when switching.
627: If you want to optimize the campaign for spending, you must set the optimizationTargetType to a target type.
628: Setting the optimizationTargetType to one of the following keeps a campaign in manual bidding mode:

634: ENHANCED_CONVERSION

654: The target cost bidding model enables you to set either a target cost per event or a desired optimal average cost per action. An event can be either an impression, click, or video view. LinkedIn maximizes the number of actions while maintaining the lifetime average cost per result around the advertiser specified target cost. A cost deviation range around the target cost can then be adjusted accordingly.

688: LinkedIn delivers better results by mapping existing optimizations against a new, more complete set of objectives.
689: Bidding for objectives: Bid types, including automated bidding and maximum CPC bids, are aligned to your objective to bid more aggressively against audience more likely to take the action based on that objective.
690: Creative optimization for objectives: LinkedIn optimizes ads and creatives in rotation in order to better deliver on an advertiser’s objective.

1139: Connected Television Only Ad Campaigns
1140: To create a Connected Television Only Ad campaign, there are several constraints on the following:
1141: Optimization Target Type can't be manual bidding.
1142: Objective Type must be Brand Awareness.
1143: EnableAudienceNetwork (LAN Enabled-) must be true (REQUIRED.offsiteDelivery()).
1144: The target audience must be locale-based, limited to the “US + CA” region, and the language must be English only.
1145: Ensure that only CampaignCreativeSelection.ROUND_ROBIN is enabled for CTV Campaign Creation.

1274: Dynamic Ad Campaigns
1275: Dynamic Ads are personalized ads that are automatically populated with members' profile photo and other data dynamically pulled from their LinkedIn profiles. APIs are available for self-service campaign formats such as Follower Ads, Spotlight Ads, and Jobs Ads. The Content Ad format is only available for managed accounts and can't be managed through the API or Campaign Manager. For more information, refer to Dynamic Ads Overview.

1279: JOB_APPLICANT

1511: Search for Campaigns
1512: Note
1513: From version 202401 onward, index-based pagination has been replaced with cursor-based pagination for search APIs.
1514: Cursor based Pagination for search APIs
1515: The adCampaigns API implements cursor based pagination using the pageSize and pageToken parameters for search method.
1516: The following parameters control pagination for search results:
1517: The maximum allowed pageSize is 1,000.
1518: pageSize governs the number of requested entities.
1519: pageToken is used to get the next set of results.
1520: nextPageToken is returned in metadata field of the search response.
1521: This should be passed in pageToken query parameter in the request to get the next page of results.
1522: Search for campaigns by ID, campaign group, name, type, and status fields. Search criteria is mandatory and can be chained together for increased granularity.
1523: If you are using the Search for Campaigns endpoint and the response returns more than 1,000 campaigns, the API returns a 400 error with the following message:
1524: {"message":"Request would return too many entities. ","status":400}
1525: If more than 1,000 campaigns need to be pulled, set a pageSize parameter value of less than 1,000 to pull less than 1,000 campaigns per call and paginate through the full list of campaigns using pageToken.
1526: This call can return both test and non-test campaigns. To return only non-test campaigns, set search.test=False. To return only test campaigns, set search.test=True.
1527: http
1528: curl
1529: GET https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{adAccountId}/adCampaigns?q=search&search=(searchCriteria:(values:List(searchValue)))
1530: curl --location --request GET 'https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{{account_id}}/adCampaigns?q=search&search=(type:(values:List(SPONSORED_UPDATES)),status:(values:List(ACTIVE)))&sortOrder=DESCENDING' \
1531: --header 'Authorization: Bearer {INSERT_TOKEN}' \
1532: --header 'Linkedin-Version: {version number in the format YYYYMM}' \
1533: --header 'X-Restli-Protocol-Version: 2.0.0'
1534: Parameters
1535: Field Name
1536: Required
1537: Description
1538: search.campaignGroup.values
1539: no
1540: Searches for campaigns associated with the provided sponsored CampaignGroup URNs list. Example: urn:li:sponsoredCampaignGroup:{campaignGroupId}.
1541: search.associatedEntity.values
1542: no
1543: Searches for campaigns by associated entity.
1544: search.id.values
1545: no
1546: Searches for campaign by ID. Example: urn:li:sponsoredCampaign:{campaignId}.
1547: search.status.values
1548: no
1549: Searches for campaigns with the provided status. The possible values are:
1550: ACTIVE
1551: PAUSED
1552: ARCHIVED
1553: COMPLETED
1554: CANCELED
1555: DRAFT
1556: PENDING_DELETION
1557: REMOVED
1558: search.type.values
1559: no
1560: Searches for campaigns with the provided type. The possible values are:
1561: TEXT_AD
1562: SPONSORED_UPDATES
1563: SPONSORED_INMAILS
1564: DYNAMIC
1565: search.name.values
1566: no
1567: Searches for campaigns by name.
1568: search.test
1569: no
1570: Searches for campaigns based on test or non-test status.
1571: True: for test campaigns.
1572: False: for non-test campaigns.
1573: Note: If not specified, searches for both test and non-test campaigns.
1574: sortOrder
1575: no
1576: Specifies the sort order of the results. Results will be sorted by campaign id. Supported values include:
1577: ASCENDING
1578: DESCENDING The default is "ASCENDING".
1579: pageSize
1580: no
1581: Specifies the number of entities to be returned. The default is 100. Max is 1,000.
1582: pageToken
1583: no
1584: Unique key representing the last entity of the response. This is to be used to fetch the next set of entities. If less than pageSize entities are returned in the current response, pageToken will be null.

1708: Update a Campaign
1709: When you perform a partial update, the header X-RestLi-Method must be included in the request and set to PARTIAL_UPDATE.
1710: Sample Request
1711: The following sample request updates campaign targeting. Targeting criteria for a campaign can be changed at any time. Modify criteria based on the current campaign performance.

1817: Additionally, you can update your campaign bid amounts and the daily budget as seen in the following example:

1938: Delete a Campaign
1939: A Campaign can be deleted. Use DELETE method to delete a DRAFT campaign. To start the process of deleting non DRAFT campaign, update the status to PENDING_DELETION.
1940: Sample Request
1941: http
1942: curl
1943: To delete DRAFT campaign:
1944: DELETE https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{adAccountId}/adCampaigns/{campaignID}
1945: To delete non DRAFT campaign:
1946: POST https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{adAccountId}/adCampaigns/{campaignID}
1947: {
1948: "patch": {
1949: "$set": {
1950: "status": "PENDING_DELETION"
1951: }
1952: }
1953: }
1954: To delete DRAFT campaign:
1955: curl -X DELETE 'https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{adAccountId}/adCampaigns/{campaignID}' \
1956: -H 'X-Restli-Protocol-Version: 2.0.0' \
1957: -H 'Linkedin-Version: {version number in the format YYYYMM}' \
1958: -H 'Authorization: Bearer {INSERT_TOKEN}'
1959: To delete non DRAFT campaign:
1960: curl -X POST 'https://api.linkedin.com/rest/adAccounts/{adAccountId}/adCampaigns/{campaignID}' \
1961: -H 'X-Restli-Protocol-Version: 2.0.0' \
1962: -H 'Linkedin-Version: {version number in the format YYYYMM}' \

1964: -H 'X-RestLi-Method: PARTIAL_UPDATE' \
1965: -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
1966: --data '{
1967: "patch": {
1968: "$set": {
1969: "status": "PENDING_DELETION"
1970: }
1971: }
1972: }'
1973: A successful response returns a 204 code.

1: # Ads MCP 2: Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for cross-platform ad management. Create, analyze, and optimize campaigns across **Google Ads, Meta Ads, TikTok Ads, and LinkedIn Ads** from any MCP-compatible AI assistant. 3: ## Quick Links 4: - **MCP Remote URL:** `https://mcp.adspirer.com/mcp` 5: - **Transport:** Streamable HTTP 6: - **Registry ID:** [`com.adspirer/ads`](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) 7: - **Authentication:** OAuth 2.1 with PKCE (dynamic client registration supported) 8: - **Website:** https://www.adspirer.com 9: - **Support:** support@adspirer.com 10: ## Get Started in One Step 11: Adspirer runs inside your AI assistant. 74: OAuth 2.0
75: OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol that authorizes a client application (like a third-party app) to access specific resources on behalf of a user, without sharing the user’s password. It’s widely used for APIs that need secure, delegated access.
76: HighLevel supports the Authorization Code Grant flow with v2 APIs. Below is the step-by-step procedure to understand and use the OAuth 2.0 flow.
77: 1. Register an OAuth App​
78: Go to the Marketplace and sign up for a developer account.
79: Go to My Apps, click Create App.
80: Fill in the following details:
81: APP Name: Suitable name for the app.
82: APP Type: Private or Public.
83: Private Apps: For personal/internal use, not listed in the Marketplace.
84: Public Apps: Visible and installable by all users once approved.
85: Note: We recommend starting with your app set to Private. This allows you to develop and thoroughly test its functionality in a controlled environment. Once you're confident the app is stable and complete, you can switch it to Public for broader installation and use by other accounts.
86: Target User: This allows you to define who your app is intended for — in other words, who will actually be using it.
87: For the vast majority of apps (approximately 95%), the ideal choice is "Sub-account" (recommended).
88: Who can install: Who should be able to view and install the app from the Marketplace UI?
89: The recommended setting is “Both Agency & Sub-account” to ensure maximum visibility and adoption of your app.
90: However, if you’re building a fully white-labeled SaaS feature intended to be exclusively discovered and installed by agencies for use within their sub-accounts, you may choose to limit visibility to Agencies only.
91: Listing Type: White-label recommended for marketing agencies.
92: After creating the APP you will be taken to the Profile section where you will need to add the details related to your APP. For eg; APP Logo, category, Company Name, APP Description, preview images etc.
93: After completing the profile details, please click on the Advanced Settings drop down available in the left pane and go to the auth section.
94: The Auth page will appear as shown in the screenshot below. This is where you’ll configure essential settings for your app’s OAuth integration, including scopes, redirect URLs, and client credentials.
95: Scopes: Scopes define the level of access your app will have — what data it can read or what actions it can perform on behalf of the user. Each endpoint's API reference page lists the scopes it requires.
96: It’s best practice to request the minimum number of scopes necessary for your app to function.
97: Click on the "Select Scope" dropdown and choose the relevant scopes based on your app’s functionality.
98: Redirect URL: A Redirect URL (also known as a Callback URL) is the destination where the authorization server will send the authorization code after the user installs the app.
99: Enter your redirect URL in the Redirect URL field.
100: Click the "Add" button to save it.
101: Client Keys (ID & Secret): In the Client Keys section:
102: Click the "Add" button.
103: Provide a name for your client key pair.
104: Upon saving, your Client ID and Client Secret will be generated.
105: These credentials are used to identify and authenticate your application with the OAuth server during token exchange.
106: Important: Be sure to copy and securely store your Client Secret immediately. After clicking "OK", you will not be able to view or copy the secret again from the UI.
107: 2. Add the App to Your Desired Location​
108: Have the location/agency admin visit your Installation URL.
109: Select the location to connect.
110: Redirected to your Redirect URL with an Authorization Code.
111: Exchange the code for an Access Token via the OAuth 2.0 Get Access Token API.
112: Use the Access Token to call APIs.
113: 3. Get the Installation URL​
114: Inside your APP Auth Pane available inside the Advanced Settings Section you will be able to see the Install Link at the top of the Page.
115: Click on the Show button and you will be able to see the Installation URLs which you will be using to install the APP.
116: Depending on your usecase and account setup you can either use the standard or the whitelabel version of the Installation URL.
117: Refer to the below steps to install the APP:
118: Copy the Installation URL and open it in your browser.
119: In case you are not logged in to your GHL account it will ask you to login to your account.
120: In case you are logged in it will show a page showcasing the accounts.
121: Select the account you want to install the APP in.
122: When a user grants access, their browser is redirected to the specified redirect URI, and the Authorization Code is passed inside the code query parameter. If you included a state value in the Installation URL, it is returned unchanged in the state query parameter.
123: https://myapp.com/oauth/callback/highlevel?code=7676cjcbdc6t76cdcbkjcd09821jknnkj&state=RANDOM_SINGLE_USE_VALUE
124: This URL demonstrates a typical OAuth callback scenario for a HighLevel integration. The code parameter included in the query string is essential for completing the authorization flow.
125: Using the state Parameter​
126: We recommend using state to protect your callback against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). Both /oauth/chooselocation and /v2/oauth/chooselocation support it.
127: Before sending the user to the Installation URL, generate a cryptographically random, short-lived, single-use value and bind it to the user's session.
128: Append it to the Installation URL as the URL-encoded state query parameter. Use printable ASCII characters only, for example a hex or base64url-encoded value.
129: On your callback, reject the request if state is missing or does not exactly match the stored value, and invalidate the stored value before exchanging the code.
130: Authorization Code Rules​
131: The redirect URI must exactly match a redirect URI registered for your app.
132: Exchange the code using your app's client_id and client_secret.
133: Authorization codes expire after five minutes and can be used only once.
134: note
135: PKCE/S256 is not currently supported for the Marketplace app installation authorization flow. PKCE support for External Authentication applies to a separate flow and does not replace the state validation described above.
136: 4. Listening to Webhook Events​
137: The HighLevel Marketplace App allows you to listen to various webhook events, enabling real-time updates and integrations based on user actions.
138: To set up webhook listeners:
139: Navigate to your app in the Marketplace dashboard.
140: Click on the "Advanced Settings" dropdown in the left-hand panel.
141: Go to the "Webhooks" section.
142: In the input box at the top, enter your webhook URL.
143: Use the toggle switches next to each event to subscribe to the events you wish to listen for.
144: For a full list of supported webhook events and example payloads, please refer to the documentation: Webhook Events & Payloads
145: Important: App Install Webhook​
146: One of the most critical webhook events is the App Install event. This event provides essential details whenever your app is installed by a user. If a webhook URL is configured for your app, this event is subscribed to by default.
147: Here’s a sample payload for the App Install event:
148: {
149: "type": "INSTALL",
150: "appId": "665c6bb13d4e5364bdec0e2f",
151: "versionId": "665c6bb13d4e5364bdec0e2f",
152: "installType": "Location",
153: "locationId": "HjiMUOsCCHCjtxzEf8PR",
154: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9iwNl5K",
155: "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gJy3W8a",
156: "companyName": "Marketplace and Integrations Prod Agency",
157: "isWhitelabelCompany": true,
158: "whitelabelDetails": {
159: "logoUrl": "https://...gif",
160: "domain": "rajender.dentistsnear.me"
161: },
162: "timestamp": "2025-06-25T06:57:06.225Z",
163: "webhookId": "1a533f85-1f1e-4886-891e-ee0cf4666e90"
164: }
165: 5. Exchange Authorization Code for Access Token​
166: Once you have received the Authorization code on your redirect URl you are expected to use Get Access Token API endpoint to generate the Acces Token which you can then use to run the API endpoints.
167: Sample Payload:
168: curl -X POST "https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/oauth/token" \
169: -H "Accept: application/json" \
170: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
171: -d '{
172: "client_id": "665c6bb13d4e5364bdec0e2f-mawqjyjd",
173: "client_secret": "74032272-7f45-4e07-8717-5e1ddbfe3de0",
174: "grant_type": "authorization_code",
175: "code": "363fe3f086e2db02bb9c34722902d21f76c9b217",
176: "user_type": "Company",
177: "redirect_uri": "https://myapp.com/oauth/callback/highlevel"
178: }'
179: Sample Response:
180: {
181: "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3MiOiJDb20",
182: "token_type": "Bearer",
183: "expires_in": 86399,
184: "refresh_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3MiOiJDb21w",
185: "scope": "calendars.readonly calendars/events.readonly calendars.write calendars/events.write calendars/groups.readonly calendars/groups.write calendars/resources.readonly calendars/resources.write",
186: "refreshTokenId": "685a9cc9f7434ae2fc66c31d",
187: "userType": "Company",
188: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9iwNl5K",
189: "isBulkInstallation": true,
190: "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gJy3W8a"
191: }
192: 6. Refresh Token Usage​
193: As shown in the previous response, the Access Token expires after 86,399 seconds, which is approximately 24 hours. This means you'll need to regenerate a new Access Token once it expires to continue making API requests.
194: However, regenerating an Access Token using the authorization code requires repeating the entire installation process, which can be time-consuming. To simplify this, we also provide a Refresh Token along with the Access Token.
195: The Refresh Token is valid for up to one year, or until it is used. Once you use a Refresh Token to obtain a new Access Token, the original Refresh Token becomes invalid, and the response will include a new Refresh Token along with the new Access Token.
196: If left unused, the Refresh Token will remain valid for one year.
197: To generate a new Access Token using your existing Refresh Token, use the following API endpoint: Get Access Token
198: Access Tokens expire after ~24 hours.
199: Refresh Tokens are valid for 1 year or until used.
200: Use Refresh Token to obtain a new Access Token without reinstallation.
201: Sample Payload:
202: curl --request POST \
203: --url https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/oauth/token \
204: --header 'Accept: application/json' \
205: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
206: --data client_id=665c6bb13d4e5364bdece2f-mawqjyjd \
207: --data client_secret=74032272-7f45-4e7-8717-5e1ddbfe3de0 \
208: --data grant_type=refresh_token \
209: --data refresh_token=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.dCiY5HiwOaxk8Cz6pQ0KstyeRu5fhPo \
210: --data user_type=Company \
211: --data redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/oauth/callback/highlevel
212: Sample Response:
213: {
214: "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3MiOiJDb21QU_Dcpo6oL_t8NN350g",
215: "token_type": "Bearer",
216: "expires_in": 86399,
217: "refresh_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.sDO9cDrBHKShX173dwDZyxh4a6U",
218: "scope": "businesses.readonly businesses.write companies.readonly calendars.readonly calendars/events.readonly calendars.write calendars/events.write calendars/groups.readonly calendars/groups.write calendars/resources.readonly calendars/resources.write",
219: "refreshTokenId": "685b558f21fa7b18e3d09a",
220: "userType": "Company",
221: "companyId": "GNb7aIvrQFVb9wNl5K",
222: "isBulkInstallation": true,
223: "userId": "Rg6BRRih7dS9gJ3W8a"
224: }
225: 7. Types of Access Token​
226: In HighLevel we have 2 types of Access Token depending on the type of APP you have installed and who has installed the APP.
227: Access Token with User Type as Agency: This Type of Access Token will be utilized to run the APIs related to the Agency Functionalities. For eg; Create Sub-Account API.
228: Sample Response:
229: {
230: "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3MiOiJDb21QU_Dcpo6oL_t8NN350g",
231: "token_type": "Bearer",
232: "expires_in": 86399,
233: "refresh_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.sDO9cDrBHKShX173dwDZyxh4a6U",
234: "scope": "businesses.readonly businesses.write companies.readonly calendars.readonly calendars/events.readonly calendars.write calendars/events.write calendars/groups.readonly calendars/groups.write calendars/resources.readonly calendars/resources.write",
235: "refreshTokenId": "685ba558f21fa7b18e3d09a",
236: "userType": "Company",
237: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9wNl5K",
238: "isBulkInstallation": true,
239: "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gJ3W8a"
240: }
241: Access Token with User Type as Location: This Type of Access Token will be utilized to run the APIs related to the Sub-Account or Location Functionalities. For eg; Create Contact API.
242: Sample Response:
243: {
244: "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJqdGkiOiI2ODViZDRiNW",
245: "token_type": "Bearer",
246: "expires_in": 86400,
247: "refresh_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3",
248: "scope": "calendars.readonly calendars/events.readonly calendars.write calendars/events.write calendars/groups.readonly calendars/groups.write calendars/resources.readonly calendars/resources.write",
249: "userType": "Location",
250: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9iNl5K",
251: "locationId": "HjiMUOsCCHCjtxEf8PR",
252: "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gy3W8a",
253: "traceId": "8f712294-b015-42a-8c69-7fcb960560aa"
254: }
255: 8. Create Sub-Account Token from Agency Token​
256: Suppose you have an Agency-level Access Token but want to run API endpoints specific to a Sub-Account (Location). In that case, you can use the Agency-level Access Token to generate a Sub-Account/Location-level Access Token via the Get Location Access Token from Agency Token API endpoint.
257: Sample Payload:
258: curl -L "https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/oauth/locationToken" \
259: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
260: -H "Accept: application/json" \
261: -H "Version: 2021-07-28" \
262: -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3MiOiJD" \
263: -d '{
264: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFV9iwNl5K",
265: "locationId": "HjiMUOsCCHCjtxEf8PR"
266: }'
267: Sample Response:
268: {
269: "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJqdGkiOiI2ODViZDRiNW",
270: "token_type": "Bearer",
271: "expires_in": 86400,
272: "refresh_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJhdXRoQ2xhc3",
273: "scope": "calendars.readonly calendars/events.readonly calendars.write calendars/events.write calendars/groups.readonly calendars/groups.write calendars/resources.readonly calendars/resources.write",
274: "userType": "Location",
275: "companyId": "GNb7aIv4rQFVb9iNl5K",
276: "locationId": "HjiMUOsCCHCjtxEf8PR",
277: "userId": "Rg6BRRiHh7dS9gy3W8a",
278: "traceId": "8f712294-b015-42a-8c69-7fcb960560aa"
279: }

71: On this page
72: Private Integrations
73: Private Integrations allow you to build powerful custom integrations between your HighLevel account and any other third-party app.
74: If you are looking to integrate your HighLevel account with a third-party app, you have two options:
75: Find and install the relevant app from the App Marketplace
76: Build your own private integration by yourself or with the help of a developer using APIs.
77: Private Integrations help you achieve #2 securely.
78: Video Walkthrough
79: Key Advantages of Private Integrations​
80: Simple: Generate Private Integration tokens from your account settings and manage them with ease.
81: Secure: You get to restrict the scopes/permissions that a developer can access on your account.
82: Private Integrations are available for both Agencies and Sub-Accounts.
83: What's the difference between Private Integrations and API Keys?​
84: Private IntegrationsAPI Keys
85: More Secure: You get to restrict the scopes/permissions that a developer can access on your accountLess Secure: A developer gets unrestricted access to all your account data
86: State-of-art: Private Integrations allows you to access API v2.0 which is state of the artOut-dated: API Keys work on API v1.0 which has reached end-of-life and is no longer maintained
87: More Features: API v2.0 has more powerful APIsLess Features: API v1.0 has limited APIs
88: What's the difference between Private Integrations and OAuth2 Access Tokens?​
89: Private Integrations, to put it simply, are static/fixed OAuth2 Access Tokens.
90: Private IntegrationsAccess Tokens
91: Generated from the UI: Private Integration token can be generated easily from the UIProgrammatic Generation: API Tokens are generated by exchanging OAuth access code for the tokens using Get Access Token API
92: Static/Fixed: Private Integration Tokens are static/fixed and do not automatically refresh unless you rotate them from the UIRefreshed Daily: Access Tokens expire daily and need to be refreshed
93: How do I use Private Integrations?​
94: Private Integration tokens are used in the Authorization header, just like other Access Tokens.
95: Example:
96: curl --request GET \
97: --url https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/locations/ve9EPM428h8vShlRW1KT \
98: --header 'Accept: application/json' \
99: --header 'Authorization: Bearer <YOUR PRIVATE INTEGRATION TOKEN>' \
100: --header 'Version: 2021-07-28'
101: Testing a Private Integration with API Calls​
102: Once your Private Integration is created, you may want to test it by pushing data to an API endpoint. Here’s an example of how to test the integration by adding a new contact:
103: curl --request POST \
104: --url https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/contacts/ \
105: --header 'Authorization: Bearer <YOUR PRIVATE INTEGRATION TOKEN>' \
106: --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
107: --header 'Version: 2021-07-28' \
108: --data '{ "firstName": "John", "lastName": "Doe", "email": "[email protected]", "phone": "+1234567890", "locationId": "LOCATION_ID" }'
109: Make sure to:
110: Replace LOCATION_ID with the actual sub-account ID.
111: Replace Authorization value with your generated Private Integration token.
112: For a full list of available endpoints and testing capabilities, visit our official developer documentation.
113: How do I manage Private Integrations?​
114: Who can create Private Integrations?​
115: By default, all agency admins can create and manage Private Integrations. You can restrict this permission at a user level.
116: Navigate to:
117: Settings > Team > Edit the specific agency admin > Roles & Permissions, and enable/disable Private Integrations for the agency admin.
118: You may apply restrictions at two levels:
119: Allow the agency admin to view and manage the agency's private integrations
120: Allow the agency admin to view and manage the sub-accounts' private integrations
121: Where can I find Private Integrations?​
122: You can find Private Integrations under agency settings.
123: If you don't find it under settings, please make sure that you have enabled the feature on Labs.
124: How do I create a new Private Integration?​
125: Step 1: Click on "Create new Integration"
126: Step 2: Give your Private Integration a name and description to help you and your team identify what it's for.
127: Step 3: Select the scopes/permissions that you want the private integration to have access to on your agency account. Ensure that you are selecting only the required scopes for better data security.
128: Step 4: Copy the token generated and share it with your third-party app developer.
129: Note: Please ensure that you are sharing the token with trusted parties only. Do not share it publicly.
130: Don't forget to copy the token generated as you won't be able to do it again later.
131: Best Practices to Maintain Security of My Private Integration Token​
132: We recommend that you rotate your Private Integration tokens every 90 days.
133: How to rotate your token:​
134: Step 1: Navigate to Private Integrations under settings, and click on the Private Integration you have created.
135: Step 2: Click on "Rotate and expire this token later".
136: Step 3: Click "Continue" in response to the warning message if you are sure that you want to proceed with rotation.
137: Step 4: Copy the new token and update it on your third-party app.
138: You will have a 7-day window where both the old and the new tokens will continue to work. After 7 days, the old token will expire.
139: During this window, you can:
140: "Cancel rotation" if your developer needs more time.
141: "Expire Now" if the third party app has been updated.
142: What if my token has been compromised?​
143: Step 1: Navigate to Private Integrations under settings, and click on the Private Integration you have created.
144: Step 2: Click on "Rotate and expire this token now".
145: Step 3: Click "Continue" in response to the warning message if you are sure that you want to proceed with rotation.
146: Step 4: Copy the new token and update it on your third-party app.
147: Note: Don't forget to copy the token generated as you won't be able to do it again later.
148: Can I edit the Private Integration permissions without updating the token?​
149: Yes, you can edit the Private Integration name, description and scopes/permissions any time after you've created it.
150: How:
151: Navigate to Private Integrations under settings, and select "Edit" from the three-dot menu.
152: Update the Private Integration name and description if required. Click on "Next".
153: If required, update the scopes/permissions that you want the private integration to have access to on your account. Ensure that you are selecting only the required scopes for better data security. Click on "Update" to save the updates made.
154: Note: Updating the Private Integration details does not generate a new token. The existing token will continue to work.
155: How do I delete the Private Integration once I no longer need it?​
156: You can delete the Private Integration once you are no longer using the third-party app.
157: To do so, navigate to Private Integrations under settings, and select "Delete" from the three-dot menu.

69: On this page
70: HighLevel MCP Server
71: Stop clicking. Start asking.
72: Your next booking, follow-up, or invoice can start with a sentence. Connect HighLevel to your AI assistant, then ask it to find a contact, book an appointment, send a message, update a deal, or schedule a social post. The assistant works directly with your HighLevel account, so you can get work done from the conversation you’re already having.
73: More than 700 actions across 38 HighLevel features give you room to hand off everyday work:
74: Follow up while the context is fresh. Look up a lead’s messages, check their appointments, and send your reply from the same chat.
75: Turn a decision into action. Create and send an invoice, update a deal, or add a follow-up task without opening each record yourself.
76: Keep marketing moving. Schedule social posts, review email campaign results, and manage promotions.
77: Skip screen navigation. The assistant searches and updates records directly, without opening HighLevel pages or reading screenshots. See why use MCP.
78: Keep access on your terms. Connect the sub-accounts you want to use and approve the permissions. Agencies with multi-sub-account installation enabled can switch between connected sub-accounts in one chat.
79: No API key to create or paste. Sign in with your HighLevel login, connect your sub-account, and try your first request.
80: One request, from lookup to follow-up​
81: “Find open deals in the Sales Pipeline worth more than $5,000. Show me the largest first, then add a follow-up task for Friday to each contact.”
82: That request connects your pipeline to your follow-up work. The assistant can find the matching deals, use their linked contacts to create tasks, and report the results in your chat. You supply the goal; it handles the lookups and individual actions.
83: Hand off whole jobs​
84: You can ask for work that spans several parts of HighLevel:
85: Prepare for a customer conversation: “Catch me up on Jane Cooper: her latest messages, upcoming appointments, open deals, and unpaid invoices.”
86: Turn interest into a booking: “Find an open consultation slot next week, book Jane Cooper, then text her the appointment details.”
87: Finish the sale: “Create and send Jane Cooper an invoice for three coaching sessions at $150 each, then mark her deal as won.”
88: Launch a promotion: “Schedule these three posts on our connected Facebook account for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 9 a.m., and create a 20% coupon for the promotion.”
89: Build follow-up that keeps working: “Draft a welcome workflow for consultation requests: tag the contact, send a welcome SMS, wait one day, then create a follow-up task.”
90: The assistant combines supported actions to carry out the request. It may need details such as the calendar, recipient, or sending account; required permissions and existing product setup still apply. Each action runs separately, so review its results when a job has several steps.
91: Why use MCP instead of asking AI to click through HighLevel?​
92: Give your assistant a direct connection to the work. With MCP, it can ask HighLevel for records and act on the results without navigating menus, opening each contact, or scrolling through screens.
93: For a request like “Find Jane, book her consultation, and text her the details,” the assistant can look up her contact, check calendar availability, create the appointment, and send the message through HighLevel’s supported operations. That removes the page navigation between those steps.
94: What matters to youAI using the HighLevel interfaceHighLevel MCP Server
95: Getting the work doneNavigates pages and interacts with on-screen controlsCalls supported HighLevel actions directly, with no app pages to load
96: Finding the right recordsUses the search and lists exposed in the interfaceUses record searches and filters where supported; can fetch further pages of results
97: Working with detailsReads values from the interfaceReceives record details directly and uses those records in the next action
98: When the layout changesMay need to adjust to moved buttons, menus, or dialogsCalls API operations independently of the app’s visual layout
99: Controlling accessWorks through the browser session’s accessUses the connection’s approved permissions and checks the selected sub-account for each execution
100: Reviewing a changeDepends on the assistant and the screen’s controlsSupports a preview of the proposed request before the action is sent
101: Use MCP for the everyday work in the capability table: looking up information, updating records, booking, messaging, and managing your business from chat. Browser use remains useful for visual work or features the connection doesn’t expose.
102: Previews show the proposed request; they don’t guarantee the action will succeed. Approval prompts and how results appear depend on your assistant.
103: Get connected in three steps​
104: Add HighLevel to your assistant using the app or address below.
105: Sign in with your HighLevel login, and choose the sub-account (or sub-accounts) to connect.
106: Approve, then ask: “Show me the last 5 contacts I added.”
107: Your assistantWhat to addStep-by-step
108: ChatGPTThe official HighLevel app in ChatGPTConnect ChatGPT
109: Claude (Claude.ai, Claude Cowork)https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/mcp/anthropic/v2Connect Claude
110: MuseThe official HighLevel app in MuseConnect Muse
111: Grok BotThe official HighLevel app in Grok BotConnect Grok Bot
112: Claude Code, Codex, CursorThe developer setup for your toolClaude Code · Codex · Cursor
113: Copy addresses exactly as shown. The sign-in page is on leadconnectorhq.com, a HighLevel domain, so use your usual HighLevel login there.
114: Everything your assistant can do​
115: Start with the job you want done. Use these examples to see where your assistant can help, from replying to a lead to organizing client delivery.

197: More ways to put your assistant to work​

You can also build and publish workflows, inspect their execution history, and compare failures by step.
199: Ask “What can you do with invoices?” to discover the actions available to your connection. As HighLevel adds supported actions, your assistant can discover them through the same connection. New permissions require fresh approval; some clients may need a new chat or tool refresh.

201: Working across sub-accounts (agencies)​
202: ▶️ Walkthrough video: Multiple sub-account support in Claude.ai — watch on Loom
203: Connect a single sub-account for everyday work, or use an agency installation with the multi-sub-account option enabled to work across many connected sub-accounts from the same chat.
204: Install for your agency. When you connect, choose which sub-accounts to include: one, several, or all. The assistant can reach those sub-accounts and no others.
205: Name the sub-account. Refer to a sub-account by name, such as “in Downtown Clinic, …”. If the sub-account isn’t clear, name it before asking for a change.
206: Switch in the same chat. Ask about one sub-account, then another, without reconnecting: “Now do the same for Uptown Med Spa.”
207: “Compare how many new contacts Downtown Clinic and Uptown Med Spa added this month.”
208: Each action in this guide runs in one selected sub-account. Comparing two sub-accounts uses separate actions for each. Access uses the connection’s authorized sub-account credentials; an unauthorized sub-account is refused.
209: Availability: working across sub-accounts requires the multi-sub-account (bulk) installation option for your app. If your install only offers a single sub-account, connect that sub-account to get started.
210: Stay in control​
211: The assistant only gets the access you give it, and HighLevel checks that access every time it acts.
212: You choose the sub-accounts. The assistant can only work in the sub-accounts you selected when you connected.
213: You choose the permissions. It can only take actions your approved permissions allow, and each action is checked again when it runs.
214: No passwords or API keys to share. You sign in on HighLevel’s own sign-in page. Your assistant never sees your password.
215: Preview before anything changes. Ask the assistant to preview a change first. The server can return the proposed request without running that action. A preview does not simulate the result or confirm that HighLevel will accept the change.
216: Approve each change. Assistants that support approvals can ask you before every action that changes your data. Keep that setting on.
217: Workflows start as drafts. New workflows are saved as drafts, so nothing goes live until you publish. Review them in the workflow builder first.
218: Disconnect at any time. Remove the connection in your assistant, or revoke the app from your HighLevel account.
219: Actions affect your real account: sending a message initiates delivery, deleting a record can remove it permanently, publishing a workflow activates its triggers, and purchasing a phone number can incur charges. Try unfamiliar requests in a test sub-account first.

291: How it works​
292: HighLevel gives your assistant four tools to find and use the actions available to your connection. It can discover an action, read its requirements, and execute it without loading hundreds of separate action definitions upfront.
293: ToolWhat it does
294: list_locationsLists the sub-accounts this connection can use, so the right one is chosen
295: search_operationsFinds the right action for a request. It only returns actions your permissions allow
296: describe_operationShows what an action needs, with an example, the permissions it requires, and its safety information
297: execute_operationRuns the action after checking permissions and sub-account access, or previews it without sending anything
298: New supported actions can be discovered through the same tools. If an action needs a permission you haven’t approved, reconnect to grant it. Availability also depends on your sub-account’s enabled features.
299: One request, step by step​
300: “Find the contact with email [email protected], add the tag ‘vip-2026’, and create a $5,000 opportunity for them in the Sales Pipeline.”
301: The assistant searches for the actions to look up a contact and a pipeline, add a tag, and create an opportunity.
302: It checks what each of those actions needs.
303: It looks up Jane’s contact and the Sales Pipeline.
304: It adds the tag and creates the opportunity.
305: Ask the assistant to summarize what succeeded and include links to the affected records when available.
306: Frequently asked questions​
307: What is MCP?​
308: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to the apps you use. HighLevel uses it to connect compatible assistants that support remote Streamable HTTP servers and HighLevel’s sign-in flow.
309: Can the assistant do everything I can do in HighLevel?​
310: It supports more than 700 actions across the features listed above. Coverage varies by feature: for example, it can read your published Agent Studio agents, while supported workflow actions include building and publishing. Ask what’s available for your connection, or tell us what’s missing.
311: Do I need to be technical?​
312: No. If you can describe what you want done in HighLevel, you can ask the assistant to do it. Setup takes a few clicks in ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Muse, or Grok Bot.
313: Do I need an API key or a Private Integration token?​
314: No. You connect by signing in with your HighLevel login, choosing your sub-account(s), and approving the requested permissions. There’s no key to create, paste, or rotate.
315: Will the assistant change things without asking me?​
316: Assistants that support approvals can ask before every action that changes your data, and new workflows are always saved as drafts. You can also ask for a preview of any change first. Keep approvals on, especially when you’re trying something new.
317: Can I undo a change?​
318: Not automatically. Treat changes as final: deleted contacts, records, and workflows can’t be restored through the assistant. Ask for a preview first, and try new kinds of requests in a test sub-account.
319: The assistant says it can’t do something, or reports a permission error.​
320: Check the error first. A missing-permission error may require disconnecting and reconnecting to approve new permissions; refreshing the connection doesn’t expand its existing grants. An action can also be unavailable because the sub-account isn’t authorized, the feature isn’t enabled, or a required service isn’t connected.
321: Can the assistant upload a file I attached in the chat?​
322: It depends on your assistant. If it can securely supply the original file, MCP supports uploading it to Media Storage, up to 25 MB per file; your assistant may have a lower limit. Chat attachments are not automatically passed to HighLevel. If your assistant cannot transfer the file, it can provide a link to the selected sub-account’s Media Storage page for you to upload it. It can also add an existing public HTTPS file by link; that mode keeps the file externally hosted.
323: Is this the same as the Developer MCP Server?​
324: No. This server connects AI assistants to the data in your HighLevel sub-accounts. The Marketplace Developer MCP Server is a separate tool that helps developers build and release Marketplace apps.
325: Try it with a real task​
326: Connect your assistant, then start with a lookup:
327: “Find Jane Cooper and summarize her latest messages, next appointment, and open deals.”
328: Then put that context to work:
329: “Add a follow-up task for Friday and draft a reply for me to review.”

162: Frequently asked questions
163: Is there a long-term contract?
164: No. HighLevel operates on a month-to-month basis. There are no long-term contracts, and you can upgrade, downgrade, or cancel your account at any time directly from your dashboard.
165: Does HighLevel replace other tools I’m using?
166: Yes! HighLevel is an all-in-one platform designed to replace multiple subscriptions you're probably paying for now. Most users replace their CRM, funnel builder, email marketing software, appointment scheduler, SMS marketing tools, and review management software just to name a few. Consolidating these into HighLevel often saves agencies hundreds if not thousands of dollars per month.
167: Is there a free trial?
168: Yes, we offer a 14-day free trial. You get full access to the features of your chosen tier so you can set up your account, build funnels, and test automations before you pay a dime.
169: Do I need to be tech-savvy to use HighLevel?
170: No! While HighLevel is a powerful enterprise-grade tool, it is built with usability in mind. We provide extensive support (especially when you're just getting started), a "Snapshot" library of pre-built accounts for various industries (like Real Estate, Dentists and Gyms), and a massive community of users to help you get started quickly without any technical knowledge.
171: What is the main difference between the Starter and Unlimited plans?
172: The primary difference is the number of "Sub-Accounts" you can manage. The Agency Starter ($97/mo) includes 3 Sub-Accounts, making it perfect for a single business owner or a new agency. The Agency Unlimited ($297/mo) includes unlimited Sub-Accounts, allowing you to scale your agency and add as many clients as you want without your software costs increasing.
173: What is "SaaS Mode" on the Pro Plan ($497/mo)?
174: SaaS Mode transforms HighLevel into your own sellable software product. It allows you to sell subscriptions directly from your website, automatically creating client accounts without any manual work from you. You set the price, the system handles the setup, and you earn additional recurring revenue by automatically rebilling for SMS, email usage, and other popular features like WordPress hosting.
175: What does "Unlimited" actually cover?
176: On all plans, you get unlimited contacts and unlimited users (team members). On the Agency Starter plan, you are limited to 3 Sub-Accounts. On the Unlimited and Pro plans, you also get unlimited Sub-Accounts.
177: Can I use my own domain and branding?
178: Yes. You can connect custom domains for all your funnels and websites. Plus, you have the ability to white-label the desktop web app, meaning your clients see your logo and branding when they log in, not HighLevel's.
179: Are there any hidden fees?
180: Your subscription covers the platform features, but there are usage-based costs for telecommunications and AI services, which are standard across the industry. This includes charges for phone numbers, SMS (text messaging), emails sent, and premium AI usage. On the Unlimited and Pro plans, you can "rebill" these costs to your clients, often adding a markup to create your own profit.
181: Can I switch plans later?
182: Absolutely! You can upgrade from Starter to Unlimited (or Pro) as you sign more clients. If you upgrade mid-month, you will only be charged the prorated difference. You can also downgrade if your needs change.

Results, performance, cost savings, and efficiencies vary based on use case, configuration, and business practices. References to “AI Employee,” “automation,” or “unlimited” features describe platform functionality and access only.

20: Install a client library
21: You can call the Marketing API with whatever you normally use to make HTTP
22: requests, but a client library
23: handles authentication and response parsing for you. Install the one for your
24: language:
25: cURLTypeScriptPythonGoJavaC#PHPRubySwiftRust
26: # No client installation necessary; just using curl
27: Make your first API call
28: To test that you have everything set up correctly, we’ll make a simple request to the Ping endpoint. Hitting this endpoint acts as a health check on the Mailchimp API service; it won’t affect your account in any way.
29: cURLTypeScriptPythonGoJavaC#PHPRubySwiftRust
30: # install jq: https://stedolan.github.io/jq/download/
31: apikey="YOUR_API_KEY"
32: curl -sS \
33: "https://api.mailchimp.com/3.0/ping" \
34: --user "anystring:${apikey}" | jq -r
35: If everything was set up correctly and the request to ping was a success, the response should look like the following:
36: {
37: "health_status": "Everything's Chimpy!"
38: }
39: Next steps
40: Now that you’re successfully making authenticated requests to the API with your API key and client library of choice, you’re ready to dive into the Mailchimp Marketing API.
41: The first thing you may want to do is learn how to import and export contacts between your application and a Mailchimp audience. You may also want to familiarize yourself with the Marketing API docs, which outline some of the common conventions you’ll run into across the API, or browse the extensive API Reference documentation.

777: FAQs
778: How do I switch to a different plan?
779: You can switch to a new plan at any time by going to the Billing page in your account. Select the plan you’d like to switch to and immediately start using new features.
780: Change Your Pricing Plan
781: What payment methods do you offer?
782: We accept all major credit cards, PayPal, and (in select countries) direct debit. We also support transactions in a range of currencies.
783: What happens if I hit the contact or sending limit?
784: After your Free Trial, if you hit your contact or sending limit, Mailchimp will automatically bill you for your overages. As long as you pay for your overages on time, we will not stop your campaigns or pause your account. In addition, if your audience size grows to (or email sends reach) the point where it would be more cost effective for you to be in a different contact tier during your Free Trial, Mailchimp may upgrade your contact tier so you are in a more economical tier when billing begins.
785: Do you have pricing for high-volume email senders?
786: We do indeed. If you have more than 200,000 contacts, we have a high-volume plan that can meet your needs.

42: Authentication
43: Klaviyo provides 3 methods of authentication including private key authentication and OAuth (used to call server-side APIs) and public key authentication (used to call client-side APIs). Read below for a quick overview of each method.
44: Private key authentication
45: All /api endpoints use private API keys with API key scopes to authenticate requests. If you do not use an API key for your requests, or if you use a key from the wrong account, your call will return an error. A 401 error indicates an invalid or missing API key.
46: Private key authentication for /api endpoints is performed by setting the following request header:
47: Copy
48: Authorization: Klaviyo-API-Key your-private-api-key
49: OAuth
50: If you are a tech partner integrating with Klaviyo, we recommend using OAuth to authenticate your app. OAuth offers multiple benefits over a private key integration, including security, usability, and improved rate limits. Check out our guide on setting up OAuth.
51: Public key authentication
52: All /client endpoints are designed to only be called from publicly-browseable client-side environments and use public API keys to authorize and route requests. Your public API key is your 6-character company ID, also known as a site ID. We recommend using the Klaviyo object or our mobile SDKs for interacting with our client-side APIs.
53: Public API keys are passed to /client endpoints using a query parameter:
54: Copy
55: curl --request POST \
56: --url 'https://a.klaviyo.com/client/events/?company_id=COMPANY_ID'
57: --header 'Content-Type: application/json'
58: --data '{DATA}'
59: Client endpoints are specifically designed to limit functionality to object creation of specific types of objects and do not respond with any potentially sensitive response data. For security reasons, this data must be accessed using private key endpoints only (i.e., /api).
60: API key scopes
61: Klaviyo's APIs support the use of API scopes, which allow you to restrict access for third parties using a private API key. Adding a scope helps you protect your and your customers’ data by limiting what third parties can access.
62: You can add any of the following scopes to any new private API key in Klaviyo:
63: Read-only
64: Only allows third parties to view all data associated with the endpoint
65: Full
66: Allows third parties to create, delete, or make changes to anything associated with that endpoint (set by default)
67: Custom
68: Allows you to decide how much access to give the third party
69: Note that you cannot add a scope to an existing private key. You also cannot edit a private API key after it’s been created. If you need to remove access to a key based on its current scope, delete it and then create a new key with the correct scope.
70: For more information about the supported scopes for each endpoint and how to add a scope to an API key, please refer to the Authenticate API requests guide.
71: Versioning and deprecation
72: Check out our API versioning and deprecation policy to learn about how Klaviyo handles API versioning and support.
73: Status codes and errors
74: Every response will include an HTTP status code with more details on whether the request succeeded. Check out our guide on status codes and errors to learn more about status codes used by Klaviyo’s APIs and how to troubleshoot error responses.
75: Rate limiting
76: All new API endpoints are rate limited on a per-account basis, and use a fixed-window rate limiting algorithm with two distinct windows: burst (short) and steady (long). All API traffic will be subject to rate limits, and will receive HTTP 429 errors in the event either a burst or steady rate limit is reached.
77: Each endpoint lists its burst and steady rate limits in our API reference documentation.
78: JSON:API feature guides
79: Relationships
80: Klaviyo’s modern APIs offer powerful functionality via the relationships object, a thorough set of syntax offered by JSON:API for modeling relationships between resources. This syntax allows developers to efficiently query specific groups of related resources, eliminating the need to perform redundant queries.
81: Check out our guide on JSON:API relationships for more information on how use, create, modify, and delete resource relationships.
82: Filtering
83: JSON:API’s general filtering syntax and its supported operations can be used across all new APIs. Please note that support for specific operators and fields is highly specific to each endpoint. You can refer to the filter query parameter in the API reference documentation for specific operator and field support.
84: View our JSON:API filtering guide for a list of the filter operations and comparison literals.
85: The filtering syntax for Klaviyo’s new APIs uses the ?filter query parameter for all endpoints that support filter operations.
86: Sorting
87: Where supported, sorting is handled using the ?sort query parameter followed by a field name. Reverse sorting is specified using a - prefix.
88: Example
89: GET /api/events/?sort=datetime sorts events by datetime ascending; GET /api/events/?sort=-datetime sorts by datetime descending.
90: For more examples, view our JSON:API sorting guide.
91: Sparse fieldsets
92: Several endpoints support sparse fieldsets to allow developers to select only requested fields of resources, rather than having to retrieve entire resources (which may be very large).
93: Sparse fieldsets are specified using the ?fields[TYPE]=field1,field2 query parameter, where TYPE is the resource type from which to select only field1 and field2. This also works for included resource types, e.g. ?fields[INCLUDED-TYPE]=field1,field2; however you also need to include that resource in your request, using the include query parameter for this to work.
94: Examples:
95: GET /api/events?fields[event]=metric_id,profile_id will retrieve only the metric_id and profile_id attributes for all events returned in the response.
96: GET /api/events?fields[profile]=first_name,email&include=profile will retrieve all event fields and only the first_name and email attributes for included profile resource data.
97: To learn more about sparse fieldsets, see our JSON:API sparse fieldsets guide.
98: Pagination
99: Our APIs support cursor-based pagination with the query parameter ?page[cursor].
100: Paginated resource responses will contain a specific set of pagination cursor helper links in their top-level links object, like the following:
101: jsonCopy
102: {
103: "data": [
104: ...
105: ],
106: "links" : {
107: "next" : "https://a.klaviyo.com/api/profiles/?page%5Bcursor%5D=bmV4dDo6aWQ6Ok43dW1iVw",
108: "prev" : null,
109: "self" : "https://a.klaviyo.com/api/profiles"
110: }
111: }
112: Use these links to navigate to next and previous pages.
113: Datetimes
114: Datetime formatting
115: All datetimes across all new APIs in URLs, request, and response bodies must be formatted as ISO 8601 RFC 3339 datetime strings.
116: Example:
117: 2023-01-16T23:20:50.52Z
