1: Make API calls using OAuth | Klaviyo DevelopersSkip to content 2: This page is available as Markdown at https://developers.klaviyo.com/en/docs/set_up_oauth.md. An index of every page is at https://developers.klaviyo.com/llms.txt. 3: Developers 4: Home 5: Guides 6: API Reference 7: Agents 8: Search the docs 9: v2026-10-15 10: v2026-10-15Latest 11: v2026-07-15 12: v2026-04-15 13: v2026-01-15 14: v2025-10-15 15: v2025-07-15 16: v2025-04-15 17: v2025-01-15 18: Changelog 19: Help Center 20: Community 21: Guides 22: Partner resources 23: Build your app 24: Implement OAuth 25: Make API calls using OAuth 26: Make API calls using OAuth 27: Copy as Markdown 28: View as MarkdownOpen this page as plain Markdown 29: Open in Claude↗(opens in a new tab) 30: Open in ChatGPT↗(opens in a new tab)Ask ChatGPT about this page 31: Open in Cursor↗(opens in a new tab)Ask Cursor about this page 32: Learn how to set up OAuth for your Klaviyo integration. 33: On March 31, 2025, Klaviyo started blocking all OAuth token traffic (oauth/token and oauth/revoke) routed through www.klaviyo.com. Ensure that your integration routes token traffic to https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token or https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/revoke to avoid breakages. 34: Before you begin 35: Before you can initiate an OAuth connection, you need to create an app in Klaviyo. If each user should install and authorize your app separately, see Build a user-scoped app before you create it. 36: Note that only owner, admin, and manager roles can create OAuth apps in Klaviyo. Learn more about user management and privileges. 37: Set up OAuth with an AI agent 38: Do this with an AI agentAdd Klaviyo OAuth to this app 39: Copy prompt 40: Show the prompt 41: Add Klaviyo's OAuth authorization code flow, with PKCE, to this app, so it can call the Klaviyo API on behalf of the accounts that install it. 42: First read https://developers.klaviyo.com/en/docs/set_up_oauth.md. 43: Ask me for these before you change anything, unless I've already given them: 44: - The app's client ID, from the app's page in Klaviyo, and the name of the environment variable that holds its client secret. Don't ask me to paste the secret here. If I haven't created the app yet, stop and point me to https://developers.klaviyo.com/en/docs/create_a_public_oauth_app; that step is done in Klaviyo. 45: - The redirect URL the app uses, which must also be listed on the app in Klaviyo. 46: - The scopes the app needs (for example, `accounts:read profiles:read`). 47: Then build, following this app's language, framework and conventions: 48: 1. An install route that creates a PKCE code verifier and an S256 code challenge, stores the verifier with a unique `state`, and redirects to https://www.klaviyo.com/oauth/authorize with `response_type=code`, the client ID, redirect URL, scopes, `state`, `code_challenge_method=S256` and the code challenge. 49: 2. A callback route that checks `state`, handles a denied authorization, and exchanges the `code` (with the stored verifier) for tokens at https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token, using `Authorization: Basic `. Never send token requests to www.klaviyo.com. 50: 3. Storage for each account's access and refresh tokens, and a refresh with `grant_type=refresh_token` when the access token expires. Handle an `invalid_grant` error by asking the account to install the app again. 51: 4. API calls that send `Authorization: Bearer ` and a `revision` header. 52: Keep the client secret and tokens out of source control and logs: read the secret from the environment. When you're done, tell me what you added and how to try the flow end to end. 53: You will learn 54: After following this guide, you will successfully make authorized API calls with OAuth. You will: 55: Learn about the OAuth authorization code flow. 56: Construct your app's installation URL. 57: Request authorization. 58: Retrieve access and refresh tokens. 59: Test OAuth in Postman. 60: Refer to the OAuth endpoints table at the end of this guide for a quick overview of each endpoint, including descriptions and links to more details. 61: You can also learn about how to set up OAuth for your app with our official Build an OAuth app with Klaviyo course. 62: This guide includes code snippets from a Python example shared on our Github. You can also view our JavaScript example. 63: OAuth authorization code flow 64: Your app must use OAuth in order to be considered for Klaviyo’s App Marketplace. 65: When a Klaviyo user installs your integration, they grant your app permission to use Klaviyo’s APIs on their behalf. You will be able to authenticate these APIs using access tokens. These access tokens come from integration with Klaviyo’s authorization code flow (shown below). 66: Construct your app's installation URL 67: The installation URL initiates the OAuth authorization flow for the account. This is where users will be directed to begin the installation process of your app after they click Install on your app’s listing page. 68: When a user installs your app, the list of permissions they’ll see will look like this: 69: Redirect the user to the authorization flow by constructing the following URL: 70: https://www.klaviyo.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id={client_id}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}&scope={scopes}&state={state}&code_challenge_method=S256&code_challenge={code_challenge} 71: The URL contains the following required parameters: 72: Query parameter 73: Description 74: response_type 75: Set to code. Represents the authorization code provided to retrieve the access token. 76: client_id 77: The client ID of your app. 78: redirect_uri 79: The user is redirected here after the authorization page. This must exactly match a URL that has been entered in the allowlist for your integration at https://www.klaviyo.com/manage-apps. Note that your OAuth app must be able to support installation from both klaviyo.com and any subdomain of klaviyo.com. 80: scope 81: A space-separated list of scopes corresponding to the list of permissions that the user will be shown when they are authorizing the app. Example: scope=lists:write campaigns:write metrics:read. 82: state 83: Klaviyo returns whatever value you pass here as a query parameter in the redirect URI. Since PKCE protects against cross-site requests, you may use this field to store any value you want to track across the authorization request. We outline how this can be used for PKCE below. 84: code_challenge_method 85: Set to S256. 86: code_challenge 87: Cryptographically random string generated by the client. This allows Klaviyo to validate that the client exchanging the authorization code is the same client that requested it and that the authorization code has not been stolen and injected into a different session. 88: Add your redirect URI and scopes to your app’s settings in Klaviyo. 89: You must use the least permissive scope set possible in compliance with our app listing requirements. If your app requests more scope permissions than necessary, it will be rejected. 90: Your app does not have to be listed to share and use your installation URL with customers. Once you've set up OAuth for your app, share the installation URL you created to invite customers to install and start using your app. Doing so will help you meet our requirement of 5 active installs if you plan to submit your app to Klaviyo's App Marketplace. 91: Generate the code challenge and code verifier 92: Klaviyo requires PCKE for safely storing credentials for both public and confidential client types. PKCE consists of a code_verifierand code_challenge . 93: code_verifier 94: code_challenge 95: A high-entropy cryptographic random string with a length between 43 and 128 characters. Can contain letters, digits, underscores, periods, hyphens, or tildes. This should be unique for every authorization request. 96: The code verifier SHA-256 encoded 97: Below are examples showing how to create the code_challenge and code_verifier: 98: pythonCopy 99: def generate_code_challenge(): 100: verifier_bytes = os.urandom(32) 101: code_verifier = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(verifier_bytes).rstrip(b'=').decode('utf-8') 102: challenge_bytes = hashlib.sha256(code_verifier.encode()).digest() 103: code_challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(challenge_bytes).rstrip(b'=').decode('utf-8') 104: return code_verifier, code_challenge 105: javascriptCopy 106: let crypto; 107: // use node:crypto if your version of node supports it 108: try { 109: crypto = require('node:crypto'); 110: } catch (error) { 111: crypto = require('crypto'); 112: } 113: function generateCodes() { 114: const base64URLEncode = (str) => { 115: return str.toString('base64') 116: .replace(/\+/g, '-') 117: .replace(/\//g, '_') 118: .replace(/=/g, ''); 119: } 120: const verifier = base64URLEncode(crypto.randomBytes(32)); 121: const sha256 = (buffer) => { 122: return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(buffer).digest(); 123: } 124: const challenge = base64URLEncode(sha256(verifier)); 125: return { 126: codeVerifier: verifier, 127: codeChallenge: challenge 128: } 129: } 130: PHPCopy 131: $verifier_bytes = random_bytes(32); 132: $code_verifier = rtrim(strtr(base64_encode($verifier_bytes), '+/', '-_'), '='); 133: $challenge_bytes = hash('sha256', $code_verifier, true); 134: $code_challenge = rtrim(strtr(base64_encode($challenge_bytes), '+/', '-_'), '='); 135: You are required to generate a new code_challenge and code_verifier pair for your installation URL for every unique authorization request. 136: Store PKCE values across authorization requests 137: When the user authorizes the app, the user is redirected to your redirect_uri with the returned authorization code (see Request authorization); you will exchange this code for an access token which will allow you to authenticate APIs on the user's behalf. 138: In your authorization request, you will also need to pass the code_verifier so that we can check it against the code_challenge in your authorization request. To accomplish this, you will need some way to know which code_verifier to send alongside the code you are exchanging. To accomplish this: 139: Store your code_verifier in a data store (database or cache) along with a unique customer identifier. 140: Pass the unique customer identifier as state in your authorization request. After the user has authorized your app, state is returned alongside the authorization code. 141: When you are exchanging your code for an access token, pass in the code_verifier corresponding to the code. Then, use the state that was passed alongside the code to look up the code_verifier corresponding to the customer identifier in your data store. 142: The authorize() method below generates the code_verifier and uses state to store the code_verifier as a customer identifier (see our full Python example code): 143: pythonCopy 144: pkce_data_store = {} 145: KLAVIYO_AUTHORIZATION_URL = "https://www.klaviyo.com/oauth/authorize" 146: @app.route('/oauth/klaviyo/authorize') 147: def authorize(): 148: code_verifier, code_challenge = generate_code_challenge() 149: # Store code_verifier in datastore for later use 150: pkce_data_store.update({customer_id: code_verifier}) 151: # Construct the authorization url 152: # Note how we pass in the customer_id as the state param so that we can look up the code_verifier in callback 153: auth_url = (f"{KLAVIYO_AUTHORIZATION_URL}?response_type=code&client_id={client_id}" 154: f"&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}&scope={scope}&code_challenge_method=S256" 155: f"&code_challenge={code_challenge}&state={customer_id}") 156: # Redirect them to Klaviyo so that they can authorize your app 157: return redirect(auth_url) 158: Example installation URL 159: Now that you are familiar with the required parameters, is an example of an installation URL, complete with PKCE values: 160: Installation URLCopy 161: https://www.klaviyo.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=client_id&redirect_uri=https://your-website.com/oauth/klaviyo/callback&scope=lists:write campaigns:write metrics:read&state=customer_id&code_challenge_method=S256&code_challenge=WZRHGrsBESr8wYFZ9sx0tPURuZgG2lmzyvWpwXPKz8U 162: Request authorization 163: When the user is directed to your app's installation URL, they will be prompted to provide permissions necessary for using the app. 164: Handle your app’s OAuth flow 165: Note that if the user is not logged into your app, they should be prompted to login. Once logged in, your app’s OAuth flow should redirect them to provide permissions needed for installation. As you develop your app, you should ensure that your app follows best practices, including handling OAuth flow properly for each possible user state. 166: Authorization is allowed 167: When the user selects allow, Klaviyo redirects to the redirect_uri provided in your installation URL. Klaviyo will pass the following query parameters: 168: Query parameter 169: Description 170: code 171: The authorization code that you can exchange for an access token and refresh token in the next step. 172: state 173: Klaviyo returns whatever state you pass us in your authorization request. 174: If there is an error, Klaviyo follows the OAuth spec which defines the possible error responses. 175: The authorization code expires in 5 minutes. Once expired, your app should gracefully handle the installation error by providing an error message to the user indicating that the session is no longer valid. 176: Authorization is denied 177: When the user denies authorization to the app, Klaviyo will redirect to the same redirect_uri noted above. Klaviyo will pass the following query parameters. Use error and error_description to redirect users to your site with your own messaging. 178: Query parameter 179: Description 180: error 181: Klaviyo will return an error of access_denied 182: error_description 183: The message will state The+resource+owner+or+authorization+server+denied+the+request 184: state 185: Klaviyo returns whatever state you pass us in your authorization request. 186: Users should be notified with a message confirming that they have denied the permissions needed to use your app, and if they want to install the app, they’ll need to go back and select Allow to approve them. 187: Ensure your error messages for installation errors offer enough clarity to users and allows installation to be re-attempted after it is dismissed. 188: Retrieve access tokens 189: Once the user has authorized your integration and you have an authorization code, use a server-to-server request to exchange the code for an access token. The endpoint is https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token. 190: The client secret is private and should never be in the browser; this is a security risk that can expose all of your customer’s data. Be sure to use a server-to-server request. If you didn’t save your client secret, you can generate a new one for the client via the UI and add it to your app environment settings now. 191: Structure your request with the request headers and body shown below: 192: Request headers 193: Value 194: Authorization 195: (Required) Base 64 encoded string that contains the client ID and client secret key. The field must have the format: Authorization: Basic 196: Content-Type 197: (Required) Set to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. 198: Your request body must be in this format, not in some other format like JSON, which can result in difficult to debug errors. 199: Request body 200: Value 201: grant_type 202: Must be authorization_code. 203: code 204: The authorization code that is the query parameter in the request to the redirect URL (see Authorization is allowed). 205: code_verifier 206: This is the plain-text random string you used to generate the code_challenge in your authorization request. Klaviyo hashes this value to check that it matches the code_challenge you sent in the authorization request that created this code. 207: redirect_uri 208: This must be the same redirect_uri that you used in the authorization request to acquire this code. If there is a mismatch, this request will fail. 209: The example callback() method below fetches the authorization code from the returned query parameter to exchange it for an access token. 210: pythonCopy 211: KLAVIYO_TOKEN_URL = "https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token" 212: @app.route('/oauth/klaviyo/callback') 213: def callback(): 214: # Get the auth code from the query param 215: authorization_code = request.args.get('code') 216: # Retrieve code_verifier from session or database 217: code_verifier = pkce_data_store.get(customer_id) 218: # Exchange code for token 219: headers = { 220: 'Authorization': get_basic_authorization_header(), 221: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' 222: } 223: data = { 224: 'grant_type': 'authorization_code', 225: 'code': authorization_code, 226: 'code_verifier': code_verifier, 227: 'redirect_uri': redirect_uri 228: } 229: response = requests.post(KLAVIYO_TOKEN_URL, headers=headers, data=data) 230: # Store the token info in your datastore 231: token_data_store.update({customer_id: response.json()}) 232: make_api_call_with_refresh() 233: return '
' + json.dumps(response.json(), indent=4) + '
' 234: Access token considerations 235: For company-scoped apps, access tokens and refresh tokens grant access to a Klaviyo account. For user-scoped apps, they grant access as the user who authorized the app, limited to what that user's role allows. 236: Access tokens may be up to 4,096 characters long and refresh tokens may be 512 characters long. Please plan accordingly when storing them. 237: Access tokens are valid for 1 hour (this is subject to change). Rely on the expires_in returned by /token. 238: Safely store and reuse access tokens throughout their lifetime to improve the efficiency and performance of your integration. 239: Use the received access token 240: If your previous request is successful, you’ll receive the following response: 241: Key 242: Value type 243: Value description 244: access_token 245: string 246: An access token that can be used in the Authorization header for calling the API in place of an API key. 247: token_type 248: string 249: How the access token may be used: always bearer. 250: expires_in 251: int 252: The time period (in seconds) for which the access token is valid. 253: refresh_token 254: string 255: This token can be used to request a new access token and refresh token. 256: scope 257: string 258: The scopes that this access token has access to for accessing API resources. 259: If unsuccessful, the possible error codes follow the OAuth spec. 260: Once you have successfully received an access token and refresh token, use the access token to authenticate to our APIs. Here is a template curl request: 261: curlCopy 262: curl --request GET \ 263: --url https://a.klaviyo.com/api/{endpoint}/ \ 264: --header 'Authorization: Bearer {access_token}' \ 265: --header 'accept: application/json' \ 266: --header 'revision: {revision-header}' 267: Note that this request is the same as authenticating with a private key to Klaviyo’s APIs, but with a different value for the authorization header. See information for private key authentication. 268: Safely store and reuse access tokens 269: Access tokens are designed to be reused for their entire lifetime (expires_in). Safely storing and reusing these tokens improves the efficiency and performance of your integration by avoiding unnecessary calls to the token endpoint, which can otherwise become a bottleneck. 270: Reusing tokens helps your integration take full advantage of the higher rate limits on the API endpoints you're calling, while also avoiding increased latency. If your integration requests a new token before every API call, you'll be limited by the much lower rate limit of the oauth/token endpoint, instead of benefitting from the higher rate limits of the Klaviyo APIs you're accessing. 271: Depending on your infrastructure, tokens can be stored in-memory, in a database, or in a key-value store like Redis or DynamoDB. To protect this sensitive information, your datastore must not be publicly accessible and supports encryption both at rest and in transit. 272: Request refresh tokens 273: When your access token expires, you can get a new access token by making a POST request. It is the same as your request exchanging an authorization code (https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token), but the body is a refresh token instead. 274: This is the 401 error you will receive when the access token is expired: 275: ErrorCopy 276: { 277: "errors": [ 278: { 279: "id": "653528d5-ad97-40ed-bf14-9494d4fcddc3", 280: "status": 401, 281: "code": "authentication_failed", 282: "title": "Incorrect authentication credentials.", 283: "detail": "Incorrect authentication credentials.", 284: "source": { 285: "pointer": "/data/" 286: } 287: } 288: ] 289: } 290: Use the following request headers and body to structure your request: 291: Request headers 292: Value 293: Authorization 294: (Required) Base 64 encoded string that contains the client ID and client secret key. The field must have the format: Authorization: Basic 295: Content-Type 296: (Required) Set to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. 297: Request body 298: Value 299: grant_type 300: Set to refresh_token. 301: refresh_token 302: A valid refresh token. 303: The example refresh_access_token() method below handles requesting refresh tokens: 304: pythonCopy 305: KLAVIYO_TOKEN_URL = "https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token" 306: def refresh_access_token(): 307: customer_id = '1234' # Retrieve this as needed 308: token_data = token_data_store.get(customer_id) 309: refresh_token = token_data.get('refresh_token') 310: headers = { 311: 'Authorization': get_basic_authorization_header(), 312: 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' 313: } 314: data = { 315: 'grant_type': 'refresh_token', 316: 'refresh_token': refresh_token 317: } 318: response = requests.post(KLAVIYO_TOKEN_URL, headers=headers, data=data) 319: print('
' + json.dumps(response.json(), indent=4) + '
') 320: if response.status_code == 200: 321: # Update the stored token info 322: token_data_store.update({customer_id: response.json()}) 323: if response.status_code == 400 and response.json().get('error') == 'invalid_grant': 324: # 1. Disconnect the integration on your end since the customer will need to re-authorize 325: # 2. (Optional) Trigger a win back email to the customer 326: pass 327: Refresh token considerations 328: A refresh token is issued when the app is authorized. This refresh token will remain valid until the app is uninstalled by the user. 329: Caveat: If a refresh token is not used after 90 days, it is revoked. This is to clean up unused integrations. 330: Every time the refresh token is called, a new access token is issued, but the previous access token is not revoked. The access token remains valid until it expires or the user uninstalls the app. Access tokens can't be revoked via /oauth/revoke. 331: Refresh token can only be called 10 times per minute maximum. Existing access tokens will not be revoked, but no new access token will be provided until the time window passes. 332: For a complete list of OAuth errors including refresh token errors and troubleshooting tips to resolve them, consult our OAuth troubleshooting guide. 333: Invalid grant error 334: If you make a refresh token request to /oauth/token and receive a 400 response with {"error":"invalid_grant"} in the response body, that means your refresh token is invalid. This could be due to several reasons, including: 335: The customer uninstalled your app in Klaviyo, 336: The token expired after 90 days of no-use 337: The token has been revoked by Klaviyo's internal systems for security reasons 338: The token is incorrect. 339: You can treat all invalid_grant responses, regardless of the error_description, like the application has been uninstalled by the user. Learn about revoking refresh tokens below. 340: Revoke refresh tokens 341: To protect the security of your customers, make an API call to revoke the refresh token for the user (https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/revoke). This should be done when a user uninstalls your app from your platform. 342: The revoke endpoint only accepts refresh tokens. Revoking a refresh token revokes the install, so access tokens issued to it stop working within a few minutes, even before they expire. 343: Structure your request with the request headers and body shown below: 344: Request headers 345: Value 346: Authorization 347: (Required) Base 64 encoded string that contains the client ID and client secret key. The field must have the format: Authorization: Basic 348: Content-Type 349: (Required) Set to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. 350: Your request body must be in this format, not in some other format like JSON, which can result in difficult to debug errors. 351: Request body 352: Value 353: token_type_hint 354: (Optional) Set to refresh_token. 355: token 356: The refresh token to be revoked. 357: The example revoke_refresh_token() method below calls the revoke endpoint to remove a refresh token: 358: pythonCopy 359: def revoke_refresh_token(): 360: url = "https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/revoke" 361: headers = { 362: "Authorization": get_basic_authorization_header(), 363: "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" 364: } 365: data = { 366: "token_type_hint": "refresh_token", 367: "token": refresh_token 368: } 369: response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=data) 370: After the refresh token is revoked for an account, the app should be removed from the account’s integration page in Klaviyo, and the user can re-install it if they wish. 371: Learn about how to set up your app’s uninstallation flow and other flows applicable to your app in our guide on handling your app’s OAuth flow. 372: Test OAuth in Postman 373: To test OAuth in Postman, download our latest Postman collection and follow the steps below: 374: In Klaviyo, navigate to the Manage apps page and click Edit on your listed OAuth app (three dots menu). 375: Your app must have events:read and events:write scopes. Copy the client ID and client secret. 376: Add Postman's callback URL (https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback) to your redirect URLs. 377: In Postman, import the Postman collection and navigate to the topmost tab of the collection. Under Authentication, add your OAuth client ID and client secret. 378: Enter the Callback URL that was previously added to your redirect URLs (step 3) as a redirect URI to your OAuth client. 379: Click Get New Access Token. Use the returned token to make an API call from the Events API. 380: OAuth endpoints 381: The table below provides an overview of each OAuth endpoint, including a brief description and its URL. Click on the links in the description to see related details in the documentation. 382: Endpoint 383: Description 384: Endpoint URL 385: GET /oauth/authorize 386: Obtain authorization from the user in Klaviyo 387: https://www.klaviyo.com/oauth/authorize 388: POST /oauth/token 389: Retrieve or refresh access tokens 390: https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/token 391: POST /oauth/revoke 392: Revoke refresh tokens 393: https://a.klaviyo.com/oauth/revoke 394: On March 31, 2025, Klaviyo started blocking all OAuth token traffic routed through www.klaviyo.com. Route calls to oauth/token and oauth/revoke through a.klaviyo.com to avoid breakages. 395: Next steps 396: For troubleshooting tips and a glossary of errors, consult our OAuth troubleshooting tips guide. Once your app has successfully configured OAuth, follow our Pass your app review and Submit your app for review guides to get your app in Klaviyo's App Marketplace. 397: Additional resources 398: Pass 30: Get AI assistance with your Klaviyo data using Klaviyo's MCP server.
31: You will learn
32: The Klaviyo Model Context Protocol (MCP) server seamlessly integrates with Klaviyo’s APIs, enabling AI clients to interact with your Klaviyo data. This page introduces the MCP server and what you can do with it. When you’re ready to get started, use the pages in this section to connect the server to your MCP client and explore the available tools.
33: What is MCP?
34: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that helps AI models securely interface with different data sources and tools. You’ll connect Klaviyo’s MCP server to an MCP client, i.e., an AI agent like Claude or Cursor, to get assistance with your Klaviyo data. Your MCP client can help with a variety of tasks from campaign creation to flow performance reports. Here’s some examples of prompts you can give:
35: “Show me the performance of my email campaigns from the last 30 days.”
36: “Which flows are performing the best in terms of conversions?”
37: “Create an email campaign promoting our Memorial Day sale.”
38: Here’s an example of an MCP client working on a Klaviyo-related task using Klaviyo’s MCP tools:
39: In this section
40: Connect to the MCP server — configure your MCP client for the remote-hosted server (recommended) or the local server, and control server behavior with query parameters and environment variables.
41: Available tools — browse the tools the server exposes, grouped by category, along with which ones are read-only, handle user-generated content, or are available on the remote server.

208: Public API
209: Introduction
210: Welcome to this comprehensive guide for the Systeme.io Public API. Our API serves as a bridge, enabling developers to interact with Systeme's core functionalities programmatically. It is meticulously designed to offer a seamless integration experience, allowing you to manage contacts, tags, and a variety of other operations integral to our platform. Adhering to RESTful conventions, our API ensures an intuitive and consistent interaction pattern for all users.
211: Getting Started
212: To begin using the Systeme.io Public API, you must first obtain an authentication key. This key is your ticket to unlocking the API's capabilities. Simply navigate to the profile settings within your Systeme.io dashboard, and generate a new key under the "Public API keys" section. Once you have your key, you're all set to embark on your first API request journey!
213: 🚧
214: Important security notice
215: Using the API from public pages is not advisable as it exposes the API key. This poses a significant security risk.
216: The proper approach is to make API calls from a server-side environment to keep the API key secure. This way, we can avoid CORS issues and maintain the integrity of our system.
217: Authentication
218: To authenticate with the Systeme.io Public API, your only option right now is to attach your API key to the X-API-Key header of each request. Let us know which authentication methods you would like to see implemented next!
219: Rate-Limiting
220: Our Public API implements a rate-limiting system to maintain service stability and availability for all users. Here's how it works:
221: Refill Rate: Your request quota is periodically replenished. The X-RateLimit-Refill header indicates when the next quota refill will occur.
222: Limit Ceiling: There is a maximum quota limit, which is the total number of requests you can make within a given time frame. The X-RateLimit-Limit header shows this maximum number.
223: Shared Quota: The request limit is collectively applied across all your API keys and tokens. The X-RateLimit-Remaining header informs you of the number of requests left in your current rate limit window.
224: If you exceed the rate limit, you will receive a 429 Too Many Requests response status code. This indicates that you have sent too many requests in a given time frame. Along with this response, you will receive a Retry-After header indicating the number of seconds to wait before making a new request. We advise implementing appropriate error handling strategies in your application to manage these responses effectively.
225: Using the API
226: Our documentation is your roadmap to the Systeme.io Public API. It details the endpoints available, their respective URLs, the expected formats for requests and responses, and outlines the basic constraints to be aware of.
227: Collection Pagination
228: Understanding Cursor-Based Pagination: Our API employs a cursor-based pagination system for efficiently navigating through large collections of resources. A cursor acts as a reference point, indicating the position in the dataset from which to retrieve the next set of results.
229: How to Use Pagination:
230: Starting Point: Use the startingAfter parameter to specify the ID of the last item you received. This sets the cursor for the next page of data.
231: Control Record Count: The limit parameter allows you to control the number of records returned in each request. Tailor this to suit your data handling needs.
232: Ordering: Specify the order of the data using the order parameter, with options for ascending (asc) or descending (desc) order. The default setting is descending (desc).
233: Response Structure:
234: Items Key: The response will include the retrieved data under the items key.
235: Has More: A hasMore key is also provided, indicating whether additional pages of data are available.
236: Efficient Data Retrieval: This pagination method ensures efficient and manageable data retrieval, especially when dealing with large datasets. It allows for seamless navigation through your resource collections, providing a user-friendly and intuitive way to access the data you need.
237: Updating Resources with PATCH
238: Efficient Updates with Merge Patch: Our API supports the PATCH method with application/merge-patch+json content type for efficiently updating resources. This method allows partial updates to a resource, modifying only specified fields without the need to resend the entire resource.
239: Example - Updating a Contact: To update a contact's details, you can send a PATCH request with a payload like the following:
240: JSON
241: {
242: "locale": "en",
243: "fields": [
244: {
245: "slug": "country",
246: "value": "US"
247: },
248: {
249: "slug": "phone_number",
250: "value": null
251: }
252: ]
253: }
254: In this example:
255: The country field is updated to US.
256: The phone_number is set to null, effectively removing any previously set value.
257: Selective Modification: This approach is particularly useful for selectively modifying specific attributes of a resource, such as a contact, without affecting other existing data. It streamlines the update process, making it more efficient and user-friendly.
258: Code Examples
259: Creating a Tag with curl
260: To create a new tag, use the following curl command as a template:
261: cURL
262: curl -X POST 'https://api.systeme.io/api/tags'\
263: -H 'Content-Type: application/json'\
264: -H 'X-API-Key: your_api_key'\
265: -d '{"name": "NewTagName"}'
266: Retrieving Contacts with JavaScript
267: To retrieve a list of contacts, you can use the JavaScript fetch function as shown in the following example:
268: JavaScript
269: fetch('https://api.systeme.io/api/contacts', {
270: headers: {
271: 'X-API-Key': 'your_api_key'
272: }
273: })
274: .then(response => response.json())
275: .then(data => console.log(data))
276: .catch(error => console.error('Error:', error));
277: In the next sections, you'll find more detailed examples and explanations to guide you through how to leverage our API's full potential. Whether you're looking to automate processes, integrate with existing systems, or build something entirely new, our API is designed to provide the flexibility and control you need.

396: Systeme.io has four plans based primarily on contact limits. Free: 2,000 contacts, 3 sales funnels, 1 course. Startup ($17/month): 5,000 contacts, 10 sales funnels, 5 courses. Webinar ($47/month): 10,000 contacts, 50 sales funnels, 20 courses, plus evergreen webinars. Unlimited ($97/month): unlimited contacts, funnels, courses and automation rules. All plans include unlimited email sends, unlimited sub-accounts, 0% transaction fees, and the same set of core tools.
397: Does systeme.io have a free plan and what are its limits?
398: Yes, the free plan supports up to 2,000 contacts, 3 sales funnels, 1 blog, 1 course, 1 affiliate program, and 1 custom domain. Emails sent are unlimited. The free plan never expires and does not require a credit card. Other features have lower limits on the free plan, like 1 automation rule, 1 email campaign and 500 students. If you need more, the Startup plan at $17/month is the next step.
399: Which systeme.io pricing plan should I choose for my business size?
400: Under 2,000 contacts: use the free plan. It costs nothing and covers most needs. 2,000 to 5,000 contacts: Startup at $17/month. 5,000 to 10,000 contacts: Webinar at $47/month (also adds evergreen webinars). Over 10,000 contacts: Unlimited at $97/month.
401: Is systeme.io cheaper than using separate tools for funnels, email, and courses?
402: Typically, yes, and by a lot. A comparable tool stack would include ClickFunnels ($97/month) for funnels, Mailchimp ($20/month) for email, Teachable ($39/month) for courses, and Tapfiliate ($89/month) for affiliates. That’s $245/month before connecting them. systeme.io covers all of this on the free plan or for $17/month. Even the Unlimited plan at $97/month costs the same as ClickFunnels alone.
403: Can I change or cancel my systeme.io plan at any time and what happens to my data?
404: Yes. You can upgrade your plan or cancel your subscription at any time from your account settings. If you cancel, you keep your current plan until your next billing date, then your account reverts to the free plan. To downgrade, you have two options: contact our support team to convert the remaining days of your current plan into the lower plan, or cancel your current plan, wait until your account reverts to the free plan on your next billing date, then upgrade to the plan you want

254: Use and manage tokens

256: Use a token
257: When calling the Pinterest API, include the access token in the request header as part of the key-value pair for authorization. For the key

275: Refresh a token
276: Authorization Code grants only
277: Refresh your access token before it expires-–within 30 days (2592000 seconds) after it is issued–-to ensure uninterrupted access for your app users.
278: Pinterest only supports the continuous refresh token (60-day expiration, refreshable indefinitely) and no longer supports the legacy refresh token (365-day expiration, hard limit).
279: Pinterest only supports the continuous refresh token (60-day expiration, refreshable indefinitely) and no longer supports the legacy refresh token (365-day expiration, hard limit).

347: Replace an invalid token
348: When calling a Pinterest endpoint, you may occasionally receive an Authentication failed error, indicating that a token no longer works.
349: Tokens may become invalid for a number of reasons, and Pinterest does not always notify you if that has happened. The most common reasons for token invalidation are:
350: The account user has changed their username or password.
351: The Github Secret Scanner program discovered that the token was leaked.
352: If your token becomes invalid, generate a new one by repeating the Authorization Code flow.
353: Reset the app secret key
354: Your app's secret key, the client-secret, is a unique identifier from which tokens are generated. If its secret key becomes public, you should reset the key on the My apps page.
355: Reset your app's secret key:
356: Go to My apps.
357: In the Configure tab, select Reset app secret.
358: Select Reset in the confirmation pop-up window.
359: Reveal and copy the new app secret key.
360: After you change a secret key, existing access tokens continue to work. However, you cannot generate any more access tokens using the old secret key.
361: Which grant type should you use?
362: The Pinterest API supports three grant types, which are methods for authenticating your app and acquiring authorization to access protected resources. The type you choose will affect how you generate an access token.
363: Our implementation of grant types and access tokens follows OAuth 2.0 specifications. To learn more about OAuth and grant types, see the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework RFC.
364: Authorization Code grant
365: What this type is for: This grant type is designed for web apps that access a user's data on behalf of that user. It is the only grant type that gives you access to the full range of capabilities offered by the Pinterest API. It requires user authentication.
366: Authorization Code is the most secure grant type because:
367: The user must explicitly approve the scopes requested by your app.
368: The user's credentials are never shared with the client (your app) directly.
369: The access token is sent directly to the client server, not the user's browser, minimizing risk of token exposure.
370: When to use it: Use this grant type if you are building an app to be used by multiple, independent end users, or customers.
371: How it works:
372: A user clicks a button in your app to connect to their Pinterest account.
373: Your app redirects the user to our OAuth page. If the user is not logged into Pinterest they will be prompted to do so first.
374: The OAuth page prompts the user to give access to your app with your requested scopes.
375: The user approves access.
376: The user is redirected to your app with an authorization code (passed as a query parameter).
377: Your app calls the OAuth server with the authorization code, requesting an access token.
378: The OAuth server returns an access token.
379: Your app accesses the Pinterest API using the token on behalf of the user.
380: Client Credentials grant
381: Two-factor authentication is required for this grant type. Learn how to enable it for your app.
382: Two-factor authentication is required for this grant type. Learn how to enable it for your app.
383: What this type is for: This grant type is designed for situations when the client (your app) is acting on its own behalf, not a user. This means that the access token generated from this grant type is on behalf of the current app owner. It is suitable for machine-to-machine communication, where backend services authenticate and interact with APIs without user involvement.
384: What you can access: With this grant type, you cannot use certain endpoints that provide read/write access to more sensitive data. To find out if an endpoint is accessible with a Client Credentials token:
385: Go to the API reference page for that endpoint.
386: Check if Client Credentials is listed in the Authorizations section.
387: Also, note the necessary scopes for accessing the endpoint.
388: When to use it: Use this grant type to access the API with your own credentials to:
389: Get started faster using the API and trying out the endpoints before you access it on behalf of your users.
390: Automate API calls for your developer account by setting up CRON jobs.
391: Because the Client Credentials flow does not require a manual authorization approval step, it is less secure. Make sure to store your client secret securely.
392: Because the Client Credentials flow does not require a manual authorization approval step, it is less secure. Make sure to store your client secret securely.
393: How it works:
394: Your app requests an access token from the Pinterest OAuth server.
395: The OAuth server returns an access token.
396: Your app accesses the Pinterest API, using the access token on behalf of your own account.
397: Refresh Token grant
398: What this type is for: This grant type allows a client to exchange a refresh token for a new access token before the current access token has expired, without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
399: When to use it: Use this grant type to obtain a new access token before the current one expires.
400: How it works:
401: Your app requests a new access token from the Pinterest OAuth server with the refresh token that you obtained when first generating an access token.
402: The OAuth server returns a new access token.
403: Your app accesses the Pinterest API, using the new access token.
404: Pinterest only supports the continuous refresh token (60-day expiration, refreshable indefinitely) and no longer supports the legacy refresh token (365-day expiration, hard limit).
405: Pinterest only supports the continuous refresh token (60-day expiration, refreshable indefinitely) and no longer supports the legacy refresh token (365-day expiration, hard limit).
406: Which scopes do you need?
407: Scopes are the permissions your users give your app to act on their behalf within Pinterest. Each scope allows your app to make different API requests, such as for creating ads or viewing secret boards.
408: As a security best practice, request the minimum number of scopes from your users to meet their business needs. Limiting their API permissions mitigates risk to them and your organization in case your app is compromised. Consider starting with a few essential scopes and request more later as needed.
409: Scope types and syntax
410: We provide two types of scopes:
411: Read scopes allow users to see information related to an entity without taking any action.
412: Write scopes allow users to take actions related to an entity. When requesting a write scope, consider also requesting the associated read scope if you need information about the affected entity to take action. For example, to create a pin on a board, you need the ID of the board or board section, which you can get from a read scope.
413: When specifying scopes during token creation, use the syntax
414: {entity}:read
415: or
416: {entity}:write
417: , and separate multiple scopes with commas or single spaces.
418: Examples:
419: ads:read,ads:write,boards:read,boards:write
420: ads:read ads:write boards:read boards:write
421: Available scopes
422: See what read and write scopes enable you to do with each entity:

431: Create, update or delete ads, ad groups and campaigns.

1: # Get started with the Threads API
2: **Warning:** To access the Threads API, create an app and pick the [Threads use case](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/development/create-an-app/threads-use-case).
3: This guide provides information on what you need to get started using the Threads API.
4: ## Before you start
5: You need the following:
6: ### Meta app
7: A [Meta app](https://developers.facebook.com/apps) created with the [Threads use case](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/development/create-an-app/threads-use-case).
8: **Note:** When you create your app, it has 2 app IDs and app secrets. For Threads API implementation purposes, use the Threads app ID and its corresponding app secret.
9: ### Public server
10: Threads will download media used in publishing attempts, so the media must be hosted on a publicly accessible server at the time of the attempt.
11: ### Authorization
12: Data access authorization is controlled by your app users through the use of the permissions listed below. Users must grant your app these permissions through the [Authorization Window](#authorization-window) before your app can access their data. For more details, see the [Permissions guide](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/development/permissions#t).
13: * `threads_basic` — Required for all Threads endpoints.
14: * `threads_content_publish` — Required for Threads publishing endpoints only.
15: * `threads_manage_replies` — Required for making `POST` calls to reply endpoints.
16: * `threads_read_replies` — Required for making `GET` calls to reply endpoints.
17: * `threads_manage_insights` — Required for making `GET` calls to insights endpoints.
18: [Threads testers](#threads-testers) can grant your app these permissions at any time. For app users without a role on your app to grant your app these permissions, each permission must first be approved through the [App Review](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/resp-plat-initiatives/individual-processes/app-review) process, and your app must be published.
19: Permission grants made by app users with public profiles are valid for 90 days. [Refreshing](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/long-lived-tokens#refresh-a-long-lived-token) an app user's long-lived access token extends the permission grant for another 90 days if the app user who granted the token has a public profile. If the app user's profile is [private](https://help.instagram.com/225222310104065), however, the permission grant cannot be extended and the app user must grant the expired permission to your app again.
20: ### Threads user access tokens
21: API authentication is handled by Threads user access tokens that conform to the OAuth 2.0 protocol. Access tokens are app-scoped (unique to the app and user pair) and can be short-lived or long-lived. API requests that query Threads users or publish Threads media must include a Threads user access token. Use the [Access Token Debugger](https://developers.facebook.com/tools/debug/accesstoken/) to debug your Threads user access token.
22: #### Short-lived access tokens
23: Short-lived access tokens are valid for 1 hour, but can be exchanged for [long-lived tokens](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/long-lived-tokens). To get a short-lived access token, implement the [Authorization Window](#authorization-window) into your app. After the app user authenticates their identity through the window, Threads will redirect the user back to your app and include an [authorization code](#authorization-codes), which you can then [exchange for a short-lived access token](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/get-access-tokens-and-permissions).
24: #### Long-lived access tokens
25: Short-lived tokens that have not expired can be [exchanged for long-lived access tokens](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/long-lived-tokens), which are valid for 60 days. Long-lived tokens can be [refreshed](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/long-lived-tokens#refresh-a-long-lived-token) before they expire by querying the `GET /refresh_access_token` endpoint.
26: ### Authorization Window
27: The Authorization Window allows your app to get [authorization codes](#authorization-codes) and [permissions](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/development/permissions#t) from app users. Authorization codes can be exchanged for [Threads user access tokens](#threads-user-access-tokens), which must be included when fetching an app user's profile, retrieving Threads media, publishing posts, reading replies, managing replies, or viewing insights.
28: To implement the Authorization Window, refer to the [Get access tokens](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/get-started/get-access-tokens-and-permissions) guide.
29: ### Authorization codes
30: Authorization codes can be exchanged for short-lived [Threads user access tokens](#threads-user-access-tokens). To get an authorization code, implement the [Authorization Window](#authorization-window) into your app. After an app user authenticates their identity through the window and grants your app any permissions it needs, Threads will redirect the user to your app and include an authorization code. You can then use the API to exchange the code for the app user's short-lived Threads user access token.
31: **Note:** Authorization codes are short-lived and are only valid for 1 hour.
32: ### Threads testers
33: To test your app with a Threads user, you must first send an invitation to the Threads user's profile and accept the invitation. Invitations can be sent by clicking on the **Add People** button and selecting **Threads Tester** in the **App Dashboard** > **App roles** > **Roles** tab.
34: Invitations can be accepted by the Threads user in the **Website permissions** section under [**Account Settings**](https://www.threads.com/settings/account) of the Threads website or mobile app after signing into their account.
35: ## Sample app
36: The open-source [Threads API sample app](https://github.com/fbsamples/threads_api) serves as a practical guide, enabling you to better understand the API and troubleshoot any issues by referencing a working implementation. This can simplify the integration process, accelerate development time, and ensure a smoother implementation experience.
37: ## Next steps
38: * Make [single thread posts](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/posts#single-thread-posts)
39: * Make [carousel posts](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/posts#carousel-posts)
40: * [Retrieve Threads media](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/retrieve-and-discover-posts/retrieve-posts)
41: ---
42: Full documentation index for this product: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/llms.txt

1: # Get access tokens
2: This guide explains how to use the Authorization Window to get permissions from Threads users for short-lived Threads user access tokens.
3: ## Step 1: Get authorization
4: The Authorization Window allows app users to grant your app permissions and short-lived Threads user access tokens. After a user logs in and chooses which data to allow your app to access, Threads will redirect the user to your app and include an authorization code, which you can then exchange for a short-lived access token.
5: To begin the process, get the Authorization Window and present it to the user:
6: ```
7: https://threads.com/oauth/authorize
8: ?client_id=<THREADS_APP_ID>
9: &redirect_uri=<REDIRECT_URI>
10: &scope=<SCOPE>
11: &response_type=code
12: &state=<STATE> // Optional
13: ```
14: If accessing the Authorization Window from an Android mobile system, make sure to open the URL in the native webview or browser and not the native app.
15: An example of how you can achieve this with JavaScript:
16: ```javascript
17: window.open(url, '_system');`
18: ```
19: ### Parameters
20: **Note:** All parameters except `state` are required.
21: | Name | Description |
22: | --- | --- |
23: | `client_id`<br><br>numeric string | **Required.** <br>Your Threads app ID displayed in **App Dashboard** > **App settings** > **Basic** > **Threads App ID**. <br>**Example:** `990602627938098` |
24: | `redirect_uri`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>The URI that Threads will redirect users to after they allow or deny permission requests. Make sure this exactly matches one of the base URIs in your list of [valid OAuth URIs](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/development/create-an-app/threads-use-case#settings). Keep in mind that the App Dashboard might have added a trailing slash to your URIs, so we recommend that you verify by checking the list. <br>**Example:** https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/ |
25: | `response_type`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>Set this value to `code`. |
26: | `scope`<br><br>comma-separated or space-separated list | **Required.** <br>A comma-separated list, or URL-encoded space-separated list, of permissions to request from the app user. <br>**Note:** `threads_basic` is required. <br>**Values:** `threads_basic`, `threads_content_publish`, `threads_read_replies`, `threads_manage_replies`, `threads_manage_insights` |
27: | `state`<br><br>string | An optional value indicating a server-specific state. For example, you can use this to protect against CSRF issues. Threads will include this parameter and value when redirecting the user back to you. <br>**Example:** `1` |
28: ### Example Authorization Window URL {#sample-authorization-window-url}
29: ```
30: https://threads.com/oauth/authorize
31: ?client_id=<THREADS_APP_ID>
32: &redirect_uri=https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/
33: &scope=threads_basic,threads_content_publish
34: &response_type=code
35: ```
36: ### Successful authorization
37: If authorization is successful, Threads will redirect the user to your `redirect_uri` and pass an authorization code through the `code` query string parameter. Capture the code so your app can exchange it for a short-lived Threads user access token.
38: Authorization codes are valid for 1 hour and can only be used once.
39: #### Example successful authorization redirect {#sample-successful-authentication-redirect}
40: ```
41: https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/?code=AQBx-hBsH3...#_
42: ```
43: **Note:** `#_` is appended to the end of the redirect URI, but it is not part of the code itself, so strip it out.
44: ### Canceled authorization
45: If the user cancels the authorization flow, Threads will redirect the user to your `redirect_uri` and append the following error parameters.
46: **Note:** It is your responsibility to fail gracefully in these situations and display an appropriate message to your users.
47: | Error parameter | Description |
48: | --- | --- |
49: | `error` | `access_denied` |
50: | `error_reason` | `user_denied` |
51: | `error_description` | `The+user+denied+your+request` |
52: #### Example canceled authorization redirect {#sample-canceled-authorization-redirect}
53: ```
54: https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/?error=access_denied
55: &error_reason=user_denied
56: &error_description=The+user+denied+your+request
57: ```
58: ## Step 2: Exchange the code for a token
59: Once you receive a code, exchange it for a short-lived access token by sending a `POST` request to the following endpoint:
60: ```
61: POST https://graph.threads.com/oauth/access_token
62: ```
63: ### Parameters
64: Include the following parameters in your `POST` request body.
65: | Name | Description |
66: | --- | --- |
67: | `client_id`<br><br>numeric string | **Required.** <br>Your Threads app ID displayed in **App Dashboard** > **App settings** > **Basic** > **Threads App ID**. <br>**Example:** `990602627938098` |
68: | `client_secret`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>Your Threads app secret displayed in **App Dashboard** > **App settings** > **Basic** > **Threads App secret**. <br>**Example:** `a1b2C3D4` |
69: | `code`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>The authorization code that Threads passed in the `code` parameter when redirecting the user to your `redirect_uri`. <br>**Example:** `AQBx-hBsH3...` |
70: | `grant_type`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>Set this value to `authorization_code`. |
71: | `redirect_uri`<br><br>string | **Required.** <br>The `redirect_uri` value you used in the Authorization Window request. It must match exactly, or the request is rejected. <br>**Example:** https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/ |
72: ### Example request {#sample-request}
73: ```bash
74: curl -X POST \
75: https://graph.threads.com/oauth/access_token \
76: -F client_id=<THREADS_APP_ID> \
77: -F client_secret=<THREADS_APP_SECRET> \
78: -F grant_type=authorization_code \
79: -F redirect_uri=https://socialsizzle.herokuapp.com/auth/ \
80: -F code=<AUTHORIZATION_CODE>
81: ```
82: ### Example success response {#sample-success-response}
83: If successful, the API returns a JSON payload containing the app user's short-lived access token, the token type, and user ID.
84: ```json
85: {
86: "access_token": "THQVJ...",
87: "token_type": "bearer",
88: "user_id": 17841405793187218
89: }
90: ```
91: Capture the `access_token` value. This is the user's short-lived Threads user access token, which your app can use to access Threads API endpoints.
92: ### Example rejected response {#sample-rejected-response}
93: If the request is malformed in some way, the API returns an error.
94: ```json
95: {
96: "error_type": "OAuthException",
97: "code": 400,
98: "error_message": "Matching code was not found or was already used"
99: }
100: ```
101: ---
102: Full documentation index for this product: https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/llms.txt

1: # Threads Publishing API Sample App
2: > ⚠️ We will update the sample app over time. Please note that all of the latest features may not be demonstrated in the sample app. Please refer to the [developer documentation changelog](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/threads/changelog) for the most up-to-date features.
3: You can use this Sample App to test the [Threads API](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/threads).
4: 1. Make sure that you are using the APP ID and Secret defined for the Threads API of your app. These ARE not the same as the regular app ID and app secret.
5: 2. Make sure you add your application's redirect URL e.g. https://threads-sample.meta:8000/callback, to your app's redirect callback URLs in the app dashboard.
6: ## Features
7: - **Login and Account:** Sign in through the Threads oAuth flow and exchange short-lived tokens for long-lived tokens. View your profile details and sign out.
8: - **Publishing:** Publish text, image, video, and carousel posts. Check container status before publishing. You can also publish text posts automatically during the container creation phase.
9: - **Publishing Options:** Add topic tags, link attachments, alt text, and polls. Mark text or media as spoilers. Create temporary ghost posts that automatically expire. Choose who can reply by setting the reply audience.
10: - **Replies, Quotes, and Reposts:** Create replies and quote posts, or repost an existing post.
11: - **Post Browsing:** View your posts, your replies, and posts that mention you. Open individual post details, direct replies, and full conversations. Browse available result pages.
12: - **Reply Management:** The direct-replies view includes controls to Hide and Unhide replies.
13: - **Search:** Search by keyword or topic tag with Top or Recent results. Filter by date, media type, and author username. Set the page size. Search state is retained through paging and errors. Results show returned topic tags and readable UTC dates. Read the [Search Guide](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/keyword-search) for parameters and limits.
14: - **Public Profiles:** Look up a public profile, view its details, and browse its posts.
15: - **Post Insights:** See post metrics for views, likes, replies, reposts, quotes, and shares.
16: - **User Insights:** See account metrics for views, likes, replies, reposts, quotes, clicks, and follower count. The page includes date range filters.
17: - **Quotas:** View API usage for publishing, replies, deletion, and location search.
18: - **Token Debugging:** Inspect the access token's application name, granted permissions, app-scoped user ID, issued timestamp, and expiration date.
19: - **Post Embeds:** Try the oEmbed API with a Threads post URL without an access token.
20: - **Deletion:** Use the trash button on your posts list or post details page to delete a post you own. Confirm the warning to continue. The sample app checks that you own the post. You return to your remaining posts only after the API confirms success. This action cannot be undone, and reposts are unsupported. The route allows 10 requests per minute per IPv4 address or IPv6 subnet within one app process. Use a test app and test user. View [Delete Posts](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/threads/posts/delete-posts) for permissions and limits.
21: - **Postman Collection:** Use the public [Threads Postman Collection](https://www.postman.com/meta/threads/overview) or import `postman/threads-api.postman_collection.json` into Postman.
22: ## Required software
23: In order to run the Sample App you will need to install some required software, as follows:
24: - Node.js 18 or later
25: ## Running the Sample App
26: Note: If you are using devcontainers, ensure that containers are enabled and supported by your IDE.
27: 1. Install necessary tools
28: - If you are using a [devcontainer](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/devcontainers/containers), skip to step 2.
29: - Install [nodeJS](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) to run the application. If you're using a Mac, you can install it via Homebrew: `brew install node`
30: - Install [mkcert](https://mkcert.org/) to create the OpenSSL Certificate. If you're using a Mac, you can install it via Homebrew: `brew install mkcert`
31: 2. Run `npm install` in your terminal
32: 3. Create a new file called `.env` and copy/paste all the environment variables from `.env.template`. Replace any environnment variables that have placeholders, such as APP_ID.
33: 4. Map a domain to your local machine for local development
34: - Note: Threads apps do not support redirect URLs with using `localhost` so you must map a domain to test locally this Sample App.
35: - Map a new entry in your hosts file to the domain that you will use to test the Sample App e.g. `threads-sample.meta`.
36: - If you're using a Linux or Mac, this will be your `/etc/hosts` file.
37: - Add an entry like so:
38: ```
39: 127.0.0.1 threads-sample.meta
40: ```
41: - This will map threads-sample.meta to localhost, so you may visit https://threads-sample.meta:8000 to see the Threads Sample App.
42: - This domain must match the one defined in your `.env` file as the value of the `HOST` variable.
43: 5. Create an OpenSSL Cert
44: - OAuth redirects are only supported over HTTPS so you must create an SSL certificate
45: - `mkcert threads-sample.meta` - This will create pem files for SSL.
46: - You will see `threads-sample.meta.pem` and `threads-sample.meta-key.pem `files generated.
47: - If you are using a host that is different than `threads-sample.meta` then replace it with your specific domain.
48: 6. Run the Sample App
49: - Run `npm start` from the command line.

1: # Threads MCP Server
2: A powerful Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for integrating with the Threads.com API. This server provides comprehensive tools for creating, reading, and managing Threads content programmatically.
3: [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
4: [![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5.7-blue.svg)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/)
5: [![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node-%3E%3D18.0.0-green.svg)](https://nodejs.org/)
6: [![Test Coverage](https://img.shields.io/badge/coverage-%3E90%25-brightgreen.svg)](https://vitest.dev/)
7: 🌐 **[Visit the Website](https://pegasusheavyindustries.github.io/threads-mcp/)** for a better reading experience!
8: ## Features
9: - 🚀 **Complete Threads API Integration** - Full support for Threads.com API v1.0
10: - 🔧 **MCP Protocol** - Standard Model Context Protocol implementation
11: - 📊 **Analytics & Insights** - Access engagement metrics and analytics
12: - 💬 **Conversation Management** - Create threads, replies, and manage conversations
13: - 🎯 **Type-Safe** - Full TypeScript support with Zod schema validation
14: - ⚡ **Rate Limiting** - Token bucket algorithm to prevent API rate limit violations
15: - 💾 **Caching Layer** - In-memory caching with TTL and LRU eviction
16: - 🔔 **Webhook Support** - Event-based webhooks with automatic retries and signature verification
17: - ✅ **Well Tested** - >90% test coverage with Vitest
18: - 🔄 **Modern Stack** - Built with latest npm packages and best practices
19: ## Available Tools
20: The server provides the following MCP tools:
21: ### Profile & Content Management
22: - **`threads_get_profile`** - Get authenticated user's profile information
23: - **`threads_get_threads`** - Retrieve user's threads (posts) with pagination
24: - **`threads_get_thread`** - Get a specific thread by ID
25: - **`threads_create_thread`** - Create new threads with text, images, or videos
26: - **`threads_reply_to_thread`** - Reply to existing threads
27: ### Engagement & Analytics
28: - **`threads_get_insights`** - Get analytics for threads or user account
29: - **`threads_get_replies`** - Retrieve replies to a specific thread
30: - **`threads_get_conversation`** - Get full conversation threads
31: ## Prerequisites
32: Before you begin, you'll need:
33: 1. **Node.js 18+** - [Download here](https://nodejs.org/)
34: 2. **pnpm** - Install with `npm install -g pnpm`
35: 3. **Meta Developer Account** - [Sign up here](https://developers.facebook.com/)
36: 4. **Threads Account** - Your personal Threads account
37: 5. **OAuth 2.0 Credentials** - See [OAuth Setup Guide](docs/OAUTH_SETUP.md)
38: ### Getting Your Threads API Credentials
39: **⚠️ Important**: Threads uses OAuth 2.0 authentication. You cannot use simple API keys.
40: #### Quick Setup (Automatic OAuth)
41: 1. **Create a Meta App**
42: - Visit [Meta for Developers](https://developers.facebook.com/)
43: - Create a new app and add the Threads API product
44: - Add OAuth redirect URI: `http://localhost:48810/callback`
45: - Get your **App ID** and **App Secret**
46: 2. **Configure Claude Desktop**
47: - Add to your Claude Desktop config with just your App ID and Secret
48: - The server will automatically handle OAuth on first run
49: - A browser will open for you to authorize the app
50: - Tokens are stored and automatically refreshed!
51: That's it! No manual OAuth flow needed. 🎉
52: 📖 **For detailed instructions**, see the [OAuth Setup Guide](docs/OAUTH_SETUP.md)
53: ## Installation
54: ### From npm (when published)
55: ```bash
56: pnpm install -g threads-mcp
57: ```
58: ### From Source
59: ```bash
60: # Clone the repository
61: git clone https://github.com/PegasusHeavyIndustries/threads-mcp.git
62: cd threads-mcp
63: # Install dependencies
64: pnpm install
65: # Build the project
66: pnpm run build
67: ```
68: ## Configuration
69: ### Automatic OAuth (Recommended)
70: The simplest way is to let the server handle OAuth automatically:
71: **For Claude Desktop**, edit your config file:
72: - **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
73: - **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`
74: - **Linux**: `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
75: ```json
76: {
77: "mcpServers": {
78: "threads": {
79: "command": "npx",
80: "args": ["-y", "@pegasusheavy/threads-mcp"],
81: "env": {
82: "THREADS_APP_ID": "your-app-id",
83: "THREADS_APP_SECRET": "your-app-secret"
84: }
85: }
86: }
87: }
88: ```
89: When you start Claude Desktop:
90: 1. A browser will automatically open
91: 2. Log in and authorize the app
92: 3. Done! Tokens are stored and auto-refreshed
93: ### Manual Token (Legacy)
94: If you prefer to use pre-generated tokens:
95: ```json
96: {
97: "mcpServers": {
98: "threads": {
99: "command": "npx",
100: "args": ["-y", "@pegasusheavy/threads-mcp"],
101: "env": {
102: "THREADS_ACCESS_TOKEN": "your-long-lived-token",
103: "THREADS_USER_ID": "your-user-id"
104: }
105: }
106: }
107: }
108: ```
109: See [OAuth Setup Guide](docs/OAUTH_SETUP.md) for manual OAuth flow instructions.
110: ## Usage
111: ### Running the Server
112: ```bash
113: # If installed globally
114: threads-mcp
115: # If running from source
116: pnpm run dev
117: ```
118: ### Using with MCP Clients
119: Configure your MCP client (like Claude Desktop) to use this server:
120: ```json
121: {
122: "mcpServers": {
123: "threads": {
124: "command": "threads-mcp",
125: "env": {
126: "THREADS_ACCESS_TOKEN": "your-access-token",
127: "THREADS_USER_ID": "your-user-id"
128: }
129: }
130: }
131: }
132: ```
133: ### Example Tool Calls
134: #### Get Your Profile
135: ```json
136: {
137: "name": "threads_get_profile",
138: "arguments": {}
139: }
140: ```
141: #### Create a Thread
142: ```json
143: {
144: "name": "threads_create_thread",
145: "arguments": {
146: "text": "Hello from the Threads MCP Server! 🚀",
147: "replyControl": "everyone"
148: }
149: }
150: ```
151: #### Get Thread Insights
152: ```json
153: {
154: "name": "threads_get_insights",
155: "arguments": {
156: "threadId": "thread-id-here",
157: "metrics": ["views", "likes", "replies", "reposts"]
158: }
159: }
160: ```
161: #### Reply to a Thread
162: ```json
163: {
164: "name": "threads_reply_to_thread",
165: "arguments": {
166: "threadId": "thread-id-to-reply-to",
167: "text": "Great post!",
168: "replyControl": "accounts_you_follow"
169: }
170: }
171: ```
172: ## Development
173: ### Project Structure
174: ```
175: threads-mcp/
176: ├── src/
177: │ ├── client/ # Threads API client
178: │ │ ├── __tests__/ # Client tests
179: │ │ └── threads-client.ts
180: │ ├── server/ # MCP server implementation
181: │ │ ├── __tests__/ # Server tests
182: │ │ └── server.ts
183: │ ├── types/ # TypeScript types & Zod schemas
184: │ │ ├── __tests__/ # Type tests
185: │ │ └── threads.ts
186: │ └── index.ts # Entry point
187: ├── dist/ # Compiled output
188: ├── coverage/ # Test coverage reports
189: └── tests/ # Integration tests
190: ```
191: ### Available Scripts
192: ```bash
193: # Development
194: pnpm run dev # Run in development mode with tsx
195: pnpm run build # Compile TypeScript to JavaScript
196: # Testing
197: pnpm test # Run tests once
198: pnpm test:watch # Run tests in watch mode
199: pnpm test:coverage # Generate coverage report
200: # Code Quality
201: pnpm run lint # Lint code with ESLint
202: pnpm run format # Format code with Prettier
203: ```
204: ### Running Tests
205: The project has comprehensive test coverage (>90%):
206: ```bash
207: # Run all tests
208: pnpm test
209: # Run with coverage
210: pnpm test:coverage
211: # Watch mode for development
212: pnpm test:watch
213: ```
214: ### Code Quality
215: ```bash
216: # Lint your code
217: pnpm run lint
218: # Format code
219: pnpm run format
220: ```
221: ## API Reference
222: ### ThreadsClient
223: The core client for interacting with the Threads API.
224: #### Constructor
225: ```typescript
226: const client = new ThreadsClient({
227: accessToken: string;
228: userId: string;
229: apiVersion?: string; // Optional, defaults to 'v1.0'
230: });
231: ```
232: #### Methods
233: - `getProfile(fields?: string[]): Promise<ThreadsUser>`
234: - `getThreads(params?: GetMediaParams): Promise<ThreadsMedia[]>`
235: - `getThread(threadId: string, fields?: string[]): Promise<ThreadsMedia>`
236: - `createThread(params: CreateThreadParams): Promise<CreateThreadResponse>`
237: - `getThreadInsights(threadId: string, params: GetInsightsParams): Promise<ThreadsInsights[]>`
238: - `getUserInsights(params: GetInsightsParams): Promise<ThreadsInsights[]>`
239: - `getReplies(threadId: string, params?: GetRepliesParams): Promise<ThreadsReplies>`
240: - `getConversation(threadId: string, params?: GetRepliesParams): Promise<ThreadsConversation>`
241: - `replyToThread(threadId: string, text: string, replyControl?: string): Promise<CreateThreadResponse>`
242: - `validateToken(): Promise<boolean>`
243: ## Error Handling
244: The client includes comprehensive error handling:
245: ```typescript
246: import { ThreadsAPIError } from 'threads-mcp';
247: try {
248: await client.createThread({ text: 'Hello!' });
249: } catch (error) {
250: if (error instanceof ThreadsAPIError) {
251: console.error('API Error:', error.message);
252: console.error('Status Code:', error.statusCode);
253: console.error('Response:', error.response);
254: }
255: }
256: ```
257: ## Contributing
258: Contributions are welcome! Please feel free to submit a Pull Request.
259: 1. Fork the repository
260: 2. Create your feature branch (`git checkout -b feature/amazing-feature`)
261: 3. Commit your changes (`git commit -m 'feat: add some amazing feature'`)
262: 4. Push to the branch (`git push origin feature/amazing-feature`)
263: 5. Open a Pull Request
264: ### Development Guidelines
265: - Write tests for new features (maintain >90% coverage)
266: - Follow the existing code style
267: - Update documentation as needed
268: - Use conventional commits (enforced by Git hooks)
269: ### Git Hooks
270: This project uses Husky to enforce code quality:
271: - **pre-commit**: Runs linting, formatting, and type checking
272: - **pre-push**: Runs full test suite, coverage check, and build verification
273: - **commit-msg**: Validates commit message format (conventional commits)
274: See [docs/GIT_HOOKS.md](docs/GIT_HOOKS.md) for detailed information about Git hooks.

79: Authentication
80: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
81: Twilio SendGrid supports API keys delivered via Bearer token or Basic authentication, depending on the Twilio SendGrid functionality you are using. In addition to Bearer API key authentication, Twilio SendGrid recommends two-factor authentication (2FA) to improve security.
82: API key
83: api-key page anchor
84: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
85: Authenticate to the Twilio SendGrid API by creating an API Key in the Settings section of the Twilio SendGrid console(link takes you to an external page).
86: Twilio SendGrid requires using API keys because they are a secure way to talk to the Twilio SendGrid API that is separate from your username and password. If your API key gets compromised, you can delete and create a new API key and update your environment variables with the new key. API key permissions can be set to provide access to different functions of your account, without providing access to your account as a whole.
87: To use an API key, pass an Authorization header with a value of Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>, where you replace <Your-API-Key-Here> with the API Key that you created in the UI.
88: Example header:
89: Authorization header
90: authorization-header page anchor
91: Copy code block
92: 1
93: GET https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/resource HTTP/1.1
94: 2
95: Authorization: Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>
96: Authenticated request with cURL
97: authenticated-request-with-curl page anchor
98: Copy code block
99: curl -X "GET" "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/templates" -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>" -H "Content-Type: application/json"
100: Basic authentication
101: basic-authentication page anchor
102: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
103: Using basic authentication with your account password is not as secure as using an API key. If your credentials are compromised—for example, if you accidentally commit them to version control—it is more difficult to regain the security of your account when those credentials are your username and password rather than an API key. For this reason, Twilio SendGrid does not support Basic Authentication with a username and password. Twilio SendGrid supports Basic Authentication using an API key as your password value for some services.
104: When using Basic Authentication, your username will always be apikey, and your password will be your API key.
105: (information)
106: Info
107: If you are currently using Basic authentication, we recommend upgrading your authentication method to Bearer using API Keys and then enabling Two-Factor Authentication for improved security. For more information, see Upgrading your authentication method to API Keys.
108: Two-factor authentication
109: two-factor-authentication page anchor
110: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
111: To ensure the security of your account, Twilio SendGrid requires enabling two-factor authentication (2FA) for all users. To learn about setting up 2FA, see Two-factor authentication.
112: (information)
113: Info
114: It is not possible to use basic authentication for users, subusers, or teammates that enable 2FA.
